earth-orbit-satellites.name: Earth-orbit satellites
earth-orbit-satellites.description: Small uncrewed satellites: the first step into orbit, and the first test of what space does to living things.

one-crew-capsules.name: One-person capsules
one-crew-capsules.description: Capsules for a single pilot: the first flights to carry a person into space and bring them home.

lunar-probes.name: Lunar probes
lunar-probes.description: Uncrewed craft sent to the Moon: to fly past it, strike it, circle it, land on it and bring back its soil.

sun-probes.name: Sun probes
sun-probes.description: Spacecraft in their own orbits around the Sun, measuring the solar wind and the magnetic fields it carries.

mercury-probes.name: Mercury probes
mercury-probes.description: A probe to the innermost planet, reached by swinging past Venus on the way in.

venus-probes.name: Venus probes
venus-probes.description: Craft for the planet hidden under clouds: flybys, orbiters with radar, and landers built to survive crushing pressure and furnace heat.

mars-probes.name: Mars probes
mars-probes.description: Flybys, orbiters and landers for the red planet, launched when Earth and Mars line up about every two years.

jupiter-probes.name: Jupiter probes
jupiter-probes.description: The first craft to cross the asteroid belt and fly through the radiation around the largest planet.

saturn-probes.name: Saturn probes
saturn-probes.description: A probe bent onto a path to Saturn by Jupiter's gravity, for the first close look at the rings.

space-planes.name: Space planes
space-planes.description: Winged craft that fly to the edge of space and land on a runway, carried aloft by an aircraft or launched on a rocket.

two-crew-capsules.name: Two-crew capsules
two-crew-capsules.description: Capsules for two or three people, built to learn what a trip to the Moon needs: long flights, spacewalks, rendezvous and docking.

lunar-expeditions.name: Lunar expeditions
lunar-expeditions.description: Crewed flights to the Moon: around it, into orbit about it, and down to its surface and back.

three-crew-capsules.name: Three-crew capsules
three-crew-capsules.description: The lunar spacecraft proved in Earth orbit first: long flights, spacewalks, and their landers flown and docked close to home.

sputnik-1.name: Sputnik 1
sputnik-1.description: The simplest satellite that could still make history: a polished sphere with a radio transmitter that anyone with a receiver can hear. Fly it to show the world your agency can reach orbit.
sputnik-1.historyNote: Sputnik 1 was a stopgap. Korolev's bureau was building a much heavier science satellite, Object D, but it was running late and the R-7 was falling short of its planned performance. Korolev pushed for PS-1 instead, short for 'simplest satellite', and it was built in a few months. Object D flew the following May, as Sputnik 3.

sputnik-2.name: Sputnik 2
sputnik-2.description: A heavier satellite with a sealed cabin for a passenger: the first animal in orbit. There is no way to bring the passenger home.
sputnik-2.historyNote: Sputnik 2 was ordered in time for the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution, which left the engineers about four weeks. Its passenger, a stray dog named Laika, could not come home. For decades the official story was that she lived for days in orbit. In 2002 a Russian scientist revealed that her cabin had overheated and she died within hours of launch.

korabl-sputnik-2.name: Korabl-Sputnik 2
korabl-sputnik-2.description: A Vostok capsule flown without a pilot, carrying two dogs, mice, rats and plants, and bringing them all back. It proves the capsule can keep living things alive in orbit and return them safely.
korabl-sputnik-2.historyNote: In August 1960 the dogs Belka and Strelka became the first animals to orbit the Earth and come back alive, after about a day in space. Strelka later had puppies. Khrushchev gave one of them, Pushinka, to Caroline Kennedy, and Pushinka went on to raise puppies of her own at the White House.

vostok.name: Vostok
vostok.description: A ball-shaped capsule for one cosmonaut, flown mostly by its automatics. It can make short hops or stay in orbit for days, and its pilot leaves by ejection seat before landing.
vostok.historyNote: On 12 April 1961, Vostok 1 carried Yuri Gagarin once around the Earth in 108 minutes. He did not land in the capsule: he ejected at about 7 km and came down under his own parachute. Soviet officials kept that quiet for years, because the rules for an official flight record required the pilot to land with his craft.

explorer-1.name: Explorer 1
explorer-1.description: A small, light satellite packed with instruments instead of mass: a cosmic-ray counter, temperature sensors and a micrometeorite detector. What it measures matters as much as reaching orbit.
explorer-1.historyNote: America's first planned satellite was the Navy's Vanguard, picked because it wasn't a missile program. After Sputnik, the first Vanguard attempt, shown on television in December 1957, rose a little over a meter and exploded. The Army's rocket team under Wernher von Braun, with JPL building the satellite, had Explorer 1 in orbit within two months, on 31 January 1958.

mercury.name: Project Mercury
mercury.description: America's first crewed spacecraft: a cone-shaped capsule for one astronaut, flown first on short suborbital hops, then in orbit. Unlike Vostok, the astronaut stays aboard and splashes down at sea.
mercury.historyNote: During John Glenn's orbital flight in February 1962, a sensor suggested that Friendship 7's heat shield had come loose. Mission Control told him to keep the retrorocket pack strapped on through reentry, in the hope that its straps would hold the shield in place. He came home safely. The warning turned out to come from a faulty switch.

pegasus.name: Pegasus
pegasus.description: A satellite with huge folding panels that count the specks of dust that hit them, to show how often a spacecraft would be struck by micrometeoroids.
pegasus.historyNote: Three Pegasus satellites flew in 1965 on Saturn I rockets. Their detector wings spanned about 29 meters and rode up folded inside a dummy Apollo service module. Engineers feared micrometeoroids could puncture an Apollo spacecraft's skin; Pegasus counted the hits so designers knew what they were up against.

biosatellite.name: Biosatellite
biosatellite.description: A recoverable capsule carrying plants, insects and other small organisms, to study how living things grow and change in weightlessness.
biosatellite.historyNote: Biosatellite II came home in 1967 after 45 hours, about a day early, because a tropical storm threatened the recovery area; an aircraft caught its capsule. Biosatellite III carried a macaque named Bonny on a flight planned for 30 days. After about nine days he stopped eating and drinking, NASA brought him down early, and he died soon after.

orbiting-frog-otolith.name: Orbiting Frog Otolith
orbiting-frog-otolith.description: A small satellite carrying two frogs wired up to record the organs of balance in their inner ears, to learn how weightlessness confuses the sense of up and down.
orbiting-frog-otolith.historyNote: NASA launched the Orbiting Frog Otolith on 9 November 1970 on a Scout rocket. Electrodes in the two bullfrogs' balance nerves recorded how the inner ear coped with weightlessness, and with spells of artificial gravity from a small centrifuge, for almost a week. The frogs were never meant to come back.

pioneer-4.name: Pioneer 4
pioneer-4.description: A small probe sent past the Moon and on into orbit around the Sun, the first American craft to escape the Earth's gravity.
pioneer-4.historyNote: Pioneer 4, launched on 3 March 1959 on a Juno II, was the first American spacecraft to escape the Earth's gravity. Its second stage burned too long, so it passed about 60,000 km from the Moon, too far for its sensor to trigger. It sent data for 82 hours and still circles the Sun.

zond-5.name: Zond 5
zond-5.description: An uncrewed lunar capsule with living passengers aboard, flown around the Moon and brought home through the atmosphere at lunar return speed.
zond-5.historyNote: In September 1968 Zond 5 carried two steppe tortoises, fruit fly eggs and plants around the Moon and splashed down in the Indian Ocean, where Soviet ships recovered it. The tortoises were the first vertebrates to go around the Moon and come home. Apollo 8 took the first people there three months later.

ranger-3.name: Ranger 3
ranger-3.description: A probe aimed straight at the Moon, taking pictures all the way down until it strikes the surface.
ranger-3.historyNote: Ranger 3 launched in January 1962. A guidance fault gave it too much speed: it reached the Moon 14 hours early and missed it by about 37,000 km. Its television camera and its seismometer capsule, meant to survive the crash and keep reporting, never got to work.

luna-2.name: Luna 2
luna-2.description: A probe aimed to hit the Moon: the first human-made object to reach another world.
luna-2.historyNote: On 13 September 1959 Luna 2 struck the Moon east of Mare Imbrium, the first human-made object to reach another world. It carried two balls of small metal pentagons bearing the Soviet coat of arms, built to scatter on impact. Khrushchev gave a copy to President Eisenhower.

pioneer-2.name: Pioneer 2
pioneer-2.description: An early lunar orbiter, small enough for the rockets of its day, with a camera and instruments for radiation and magnetism.
pioneer-2.historyNote: Pioneer 2 never got far. It launched on 8 November 1958, but its Thor-Able's third stage failed to light, probably because of a broken wire, and it climbed to about 1,550 km before falling back 42 minutes later. Even that short flight hinted that the radiation above the equator was stronger than anyone had expected.

lunar-orbiter.name: Lunar Orbiter
lunar-orbiter.description: A camera platform in lunar orbit that develops its own film on board and scans the pictures for radio, to map landing sites.
lunar-orbiter.historyNote: Five Lunar Orbiters flew in 1966 and 1967 to photograph possible Apollo landing sites, and all five worked. Each developed its film on board, scanned it and radioed the pictures home. When their work was done, each was deliberately crashed into the Moon.

surveyor.name: Surveyor
surveyor.description: A three-legged robot lander that brakes with a rocket and settles softly onto the Moon, to prove the ground can carry a spacecraft.
surveyor.historyNote: Surveyor 3 landed in April 1967. In November 1969 Apollo 12 set down less than 200 meters away, and Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over and brought back its television camera and other parts, so engineers could see what more than two years on the Moon had done to them.

luna-15.name: Luna 15
luna-15.description: A robot lander with a drill and a small return rocket, meant to scoop up lunar soil and fly it back to Earth.
luna-15.historyNote: Luna 15 was the last Soviet chance to bring lunar soil home before Apollo 11. It was still in lunar orbit when Armstrong and Aldrin landed, and it crashed in Mare Crisium on 21 July 1969 while they were on the surface. A robot sample return finally succeeded with Luna 16 in 1970.

luna-3.name: Luna 3
luna-3.description: A probe that swings behind the Moon and photographs the side that never faces the Earth.
luna-3.historyNote: On 7 October 1959 Luna 3 took 29 photographs of the far side of the Moon in about 40 minutes, developed the film on board, and later scanned 17 of them for radio. Rough as they were, they showed mountainous ground quite unlike the side we see.

luna-17.name: Luna 17
luna-17.description: A lander that lowers ramps and sends a remote-controlled rover out to drive across the Moon.
luna-17.historyNote: Lunokhod 1 rolled down Luna 17's ramps on 17 November 1970. Built to last three lunar days, it worked through eleven and drove about 10.5 km, steered by drivers on Earth through a delay of several seconds. Its operations ended on 4 October 1971, the anniversary of Sputnik 1.

pioneer-sun-orbiter.name: Pioneer Sun orbiter
pioneer-sun-orbiter.description: Spin-stabilized probes placed in their own orbits around the Sun, to measure the solar wind and space weather between the planets.
pioneer-sun-orbiter.historyNote: Pioneer 6 was launched in December 1965 to watch the solar wind from its own orbit around the Sun. It far outlived its design: on 8 December 2000 controllers made contact once more, 35 years after launch, the last time anyone heard from it.

mariner-10.name: Mariner 10
mariner-10.description: A probe that uses Venus's gravity to fall inward to Mercury: the first flight to use one planet to reach another.
mariner-10.historyNote: Mariner 10 flew past Venus on 5 February 1974, the first spacecraft to use one planet's gravity to reach another. The flyby bent its path inward, and it passed Mercury three times in 1974 and 1975, the first time at 703 km. The technique had been worked out on paper decades before.

mariner-5.name: Mariner 5
mariner-5.description: A flyby probe passing close to Venus, studying its atmosphere with radio signals that skim through it.
mariner-5.historyNote: Mariner 5 flew past Venus on 19 October 1967, a day after the Soviet Venera 4 dropped a capsule into its atmosphere. Scientists from both countries published the two missions' results together, a rare joint effort in the middle of the space race.

pioneer-venus-orbiter.name: Pioneer Venus Orbiter
pioneer-venus-orbiter.description: An orbiter that maps Venus's surface through the clouds by radar and watches its upper atmosphere for years.
pioneer-venus-orbiter.historyNote: Pioneer Venus 1 reached Venus in December 1978 and kept working for almost 14 years. Its radar mapped 93 % of the band from 74 degrees north to 63 degrees south, the first map of nearly the whole hidden surface. When its fuel ran out its orbit sank, and on 8 October 1992 it burned up in the atmosphere it had studied.

venera-15.name: Venera 15
venera-15.description: An orbiter with a large side-looking radar, mapping Venus's northern hemisphere in detail.
venera-15.historyNote: Venera 15 reached Venus in October 1983, with its twin Venera 16. Their side-looking radars mapped the northern hemisphere from the pole to about 30 degrees north, and American and Soviet scientists later turned the data into joint maps.

pioneer-venus-multiprobe.name: Pioneer Venus Multiprobe
pioneer-venus-multiprobe.description: A carrier that releases one large and three small probes, which fall through Venus's atmosphere at widely spaced points and radio back what they find.
pioneer-venus-multiprobe.historyNote: On 9 December 1978 one large and three small probes, named North, Day and Night, fell into Venus's atmosphere. None was built to survive hitting the ground, but the Day probe did, and it kept sending temperatures from the surface for 67 minutes until its batteries ran out.

venera-7.name: Venera 7
venera-7.description: A heavily armored lander built to survive the heat and pressure at Venus's surface long enough to send data home.
venera-7.historyNote: On 15 December 1970 Venera 7's parachute failed and it hit Venus at about 60 km/h, coming to rest on its side. Controllers thought it had died, but weeks later the recordings showed a faint signal: it had reported about 475 degrees Celsius for some 23 minutes, the first data from the surface of another planet.

venera-lander.name: Venera lander
venera-lander.description: A carrier craft and a lander travel together to Venus; the lander dives to the surface while the carrier relays its signal.
venera-lander.historyNote: Venera 9 landed on 22 October 1975 and sent back the first picture ever taken on the surface of another planet: jagged rocks on a layer of dust. A lens cap stayed on, so only half the planned view came through. The lander lasted about 53 minutes, and its carrier became the first spacecraft to orbit Venus.

mariner-6.name: Mariner 6
mariner-6.description: A flyby probe passing close over Mars and photographing its surface and atmosphere.
mariner-6.historyNote: Mariner 6 flew past Mars on 31 July 1969, about 3,430 km up, and sent back 75 pictures. They showed so many craters that the camera team called Mars more like the Moon than the Earth. Its pictures of the south polar cap were intriguing enough that controllers reprogrammed its twin, Mariner 7, in flight to take more of them.

mariner-9.name: Mariner 9
mariner-9.description: The first spacecraft to orbit another planet, mapping Mars from pole to pole.
mariner-9.historyNote: Mariner 9 reached Mars on 14 November 1971, the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, and found it hidden by a planet-wide dust storm. Only Olympus Mons and three other volcanoes showed above the haze. JPL put the mapping off until the dust settled, and Mariner 9 went on to map most of Mars.

viking.name: Viking
viking.description: An orbiter and a lander: the orbiter surveys Mars and picks the site, the lander searches the soil for signs of life.
viking.historyNote: Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976. Its Labeled Release experiment fed soil samples nutrients laced with radioactive carbon and watched for gas, and the first result looked positive. Other tests found no organic molecules, and most scientists blame reactive chemicals in the soil, but the experiment's designer maintained it had found life.

mars-2.name: Mars 2
mars-2.description: An orbiter carrying a lander, which carries a small rover on skis to step across the surface.
mars-2.historyNote: After the Mars 2 lander crashed, Mars 3 made the first soft landing on Mars on 2 December 1971, in the middle of a planet-wide dust storm. It began sending a picture and fell silent within seconds. Its small rover, meant to walk on two skis at the end of a 15-meter cable, never left the lander.

mars-m69.name: Mars M-69
mars-m69.description: A heavy Mars orbiter designed for the new Proton rocket, with cameras and instruments to study the planet from orbit.
mars-m69.historyNote: Both Mars M-69 orbiters were lost in 1969, on 27 March and 2 April, when their Proton rockets failed. The project was already late and overweight, and its lander had been dropped from the design before launch.

pioneer-10.name: Pioneer 10
pioneer-10.description: A probe sent through the asteroid belt to Jupiter, and on out of the Solar System.
pioneer-10.historyNote: Pioneer 10, launched on 2 March 1972, was the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and to fly past Jupiter, on 3 December 1973. It carries a plaque showing where the Earth is, in case anyone ever finds it. Its last signal reached Earth in 2003.

pioneer-11.name: Pioneer 11
pioneer-11.description: A probe that flies past Jupiter and uses its gravity to swing across to Saturn.
pioneer-11.historyNote: Pioneer 11 flew past Jupiter in 1974, and Jupiter's gravity swung it onto a path to Saturn, which it reached in 1979, the first spacecraft there. In 1995 its power ran too low to work its instruments.

x-15.name: X-15
x-15.description: A rocket plane dropped from under the wing of a bomber, flying faster and higher than any aircraft before it, to the edge of space and back to a dry lakebed.
x-15.historyNote: Three X-15s made 199 flights between 1959 and 1968, carried aloft under the wing of a B-52. Joe Walker flew one to 354,200 feet, about 108 km, in August 1963, and in 1967 Pete Knight reached Mach 6.7, about 4,520 mph, in the modified X-15A-2.

mig-e-154.name: OKB-MiG E-154
mig-e-154.description: A rocket plane from the MiG design bureau, carried up under the belly of a bomber and dropped, to fly faster and higher than any Soviet aircraft before it, to the edge of space and back to a runway.
mig-e-154.historyNote: The E-154 is our own invention, the Soviet answer to the X-15, in place of a rocket-launched space plane in the game that inspired this one. The real Mikoyan bureau did design a Soviet space plane, Spiral, but only its subsonic test craft, the MiG-105, was built. It made eight flights between 1976 and 1978.

gemini.name: Gemini
gemini.description: A two-person capsule built to master what a Moon landing needs: long flights, spacewalks, and rendezvous and docking with another craft.
gemini.historyNote: Gemini 8 made the first docking of two spacecraft, with an Agena, in March 1966. Soon after, a thruster on the capsule stuck and set the pair rolling. Neil Armstrong and David Scott undocked, the capsule spun up to a turn a second, and Armstrong stopped it with the reentry thrusters, which forced an early landing in the Pacific.

circumlunar-gemini-earth-orbit.name: Circumlunar Gemini: Earth-orbit tests
circumlunar-gemini-earth-orbit.description: Tests close to home for a Gemini sent around the Moon: a heat shield for lunar return speed, and the Transtage that would push it there.
circumlunar-gemini-earth-orbit.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.

lunar-orbital-gemini-earth-orbit.name: Lunar-orbit Gemini: Earth-orbit tests
lunar-orbital-gemini-earth-orbit.description: Tests in Earth orbit for a Gemini that could brake into lunar orbit: its heat shield and the propulsion module behind it.
lunar-orbital-gemini-earth-orbit.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.

gemini-direct-ascent-earth-orbit.name: Gemini Direct Ascent: Earth-orbit tests
gemini-direct-ascent-earth-orbit.description: Tests in Earth orbit for a Gemini that would land on the Moon in one piece, and its landing and ascent modules.
gemini-direct-ascent-earth-orbit.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.

voskhod.name: Voskhod
voskhod.description: The Vostok capsule rebuilt to carry two or three people, and fitted with an inflatable airlock for the first spacewalk.
voskhod.historyNote: Voskhod 1 flew three cosmonauts in October 1964, the first crew of more than one, with no spacesuits: there was no room for them. On Voskhod 2 in March 1965 Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, 12 minutes on a 5.35 m tether. His suit ballooned in the vacuum, and he had to let air out of it to squeeze back into the airlock.

soyuz-7k-l1-earth-orbit.name: Soyuz 7K-L1: Earth-orbit tests
soyuz-7k-l1-earth-orbit.description: The stripped-down Soyuz meant to carry two cosmonauts around the Moon, first tested in flights close to Earth.
soyuz-7k-l1-earth-orbit.historyNote: The 7K-L1 flew without a crew under the name Zond. In September 1968 Zond 5 went around the Moon and came home with two tortoises aboard, and Apollo 8 carried people around it three months later. No 7K-L1 ever flew a crew.

soyuz-7k-l3-earth-orbit.name: Soyuz 7K-L3: Earth-orbit tests
soyuz-7k-l3-earth-orbit.description: The lunar-orbit Soyuz and its one-person LK lander, tested in Earth orbit before any trip to the Moon.
soyuz-7k-l3-earth-orbit.historyNote: The LK lander was tested without a crew in Earth orbit three times, as Kosmos 379, 398 and 434 in 1970 and 1971, firing its engine as if landing on the Moon and lifting off again. The last test qualified it as flightworthy. It never went to the Moon: the N1 rocket meant to carry it never made a successful flight.

lk-700-earth-orbit.name: LK-700: Earth-orbit tests
lk-700-earth-orbit.description: A heavy direct-ascent lunar craft, tested in long flights around the Earth before it heads for the Moon.
lk-700-earth-orbit.historyNote: Vladimir Chelomei proposed the LK-700 in 1964 as a simpler path than Korolev's: one craft on his giant UR-700, landing directly on the Moon and returning with no rendezvous. The money went to the N1 instead, the UR-700 was never built, and the LK-700 was cancelled in 1974.

gemini-eor-earth-orbit.name: Gemini EOR: Earth-orbit tests
gemini-eor-earth-orbit.description: A light lunar lander for Gemini, assembled in Earth orbit, put through its paces close to home.
gemini-eor-earth-orbit.historyNote: In 1961 Langley engineers sketched the smallest Moon lander anyone took seriously: one astronaut standing on an open rocket platform with landing legs, good for two to four hours on the surface. Gemini's manager, James Chamberlin, later built a plan to land Gemini crews on the Moon around a lander much like it. NASA chose Apollo instead.

circumlunar-gemini.name: Circumlunar Gemini
circumlunar-gemini.description: A Gemini capsule pushed around the Moon by a Transtage stage it docks with in Earth orbit.
circumlunar-gemini.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.

lunar-orbital-gemini.name: Lunar-orbit Gemini
lunar-orbital-gemini.description: A Gemini capsule with a propulsion module strong enough to brake into lunar orbit and break out again.
lunar-orbital-gemini.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.

gemini-direct-ascent.name: Gemini Direct Ascent
gemini-direct-ascent.description: One large spacecraft built around Gemini that flies straight to the Moon, lands, and lifts off for home.
gemini-direct-ascent.historyNote: McDonnell proposed flying Gemini to the Moon in 1961, before the program even had its name. Its ideas ranged from a capsule pushed around the Moon by a Centaur stage, docking with the gear built for the Agena, to a Gemini modified to land. NASA kept the Moon for Apollo, and none of them flew.

apollo.name: Apollo
apollo.description: A command and service module with a separate lunar module: two astronauts land while the third waits in lunar orbit, and they meet again to fly home.
apollo.historyNote: Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, and Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins waited in orbit. Six Apollo missions landed in all, and twelve astronauts walked on the Moon.

gemini-eor.name: Gemini EOR
gemini-eor.description: A Moon landing assembled from parts launched separately and joined in Earth orbit, with a light open lander for the final step down.
gemini-eor.historyNote: In 1961 Langley engineers sketched the smallest Moon lander anyone took seriously: one astronaut standing on an open rocket platform with landing legs, good for two to four hours on the surface. Gemini's manager, James Chamberlin, later built a plan to land Gemini crews on the Moon around a lander much like it. NASA chose Apollo instead.

soyuz-7k-l1.name: Soyuz 7K-L1 circumlunar
soyuz-7k-l1.description: A two-person Soyuz flown once around the Moon and straight back, without stopping in lunar orbit.
soyuz-7k-l1.historyNote: The 7K-L1 flew without a crew under the name Zond. In September 1968 Zond 5 went around the Moon and came home with two tortoises aboard, and Apollo 8 carried people around it three months later. No 7K-L1 ever flew a crew.

soyuz-7k-l3.name: Soyuz 7K-L3 lunar landing
soyuz-7k-l3.description: A lunar-orbit Soyuz and the one-person LK lander: a single cosmonaut goes down while the other stays in orbit.
soyuz-7k-l3.historyNote: The LK lander was tested without a crew in Earth orbit three times, as Kosmos 379, 398 and 434 in 1970 and 1971, firing its engine as if landing on the Moon and lifting off again. The last test qualified it as flightworthy. It never went to the Moon: the N1 rocket meant to carry it never made a successful flight.

lk-700.name: LK-700 Direct Ascent
lk-700.description: A heavy spacecraft that flies straight to the Moon, lands with its whole crew and returns, launched on the giant UR-700.
lk-700.historyNote: Vladimir Chelomei proposed the LK-700 in 1964 as a simpler path than Korolev's: one craft on his giant UR-700, landing directly on the Moon and returning with no rendezvous. The money went to the N1 instead, the UR-700 was never built, and the LK-700 was cancelled in 1974.

apollo-earth-orbit.name: Apollo: Earth-orbit tests
apollo-earth-orbit.description: The Apollo spacecraft proved close to home: long flights, spacewalks, and the lunar module flown, separated and docked again in Earth orbit.
apollo-earth-orbit.historyNote: Apollo 9 tested the lunar module in Earth orbit in March 1969. With two crewed craft flying at once, the crew named them Spider and Gumdrop. James McDivitt and Russell Schweickart flew Spider away from Gumdrop and back, proving the lander before it went to the Moon.

soyuz-7k-ok.name: Soyuz 7K-OK
soyuz-7k-ok.description: The Earth-orbit Soyuz: long flights, and automatic rendezvous and docking guided by the Igla radar system.
soyuz-7k-ok.historyNote: In October 1967 Kosmos 186 and 188 made the first automatic docking, steered by the Igla system with nobody aboard. In January 1969 Soyuz 4 and 5 made the first docking of two crewed craft, and Aleksei Yeliseyev and Yevgeny Khrunov spacewalked across, since there was no tunnel between the ships.

sputnik-1-satellite.name: Sputnik 1 satellite
sputnik-1-satellite.description: A polished aluminum sphere about half a meter across, with four long antennas and a battery-powered transmitter.
sputnik-1-satellite.historyNote: Sputnik 1 only sent a simple beep, for about three weeks until its batteries ran down. Two physicists at Johns Hopkins' Applied Physics Laboratory found they could work out its whole orbit from the Doppler shift of that beep. Their lab then turned the idea around: if you know a satellite's orbit, the same shift tells you where you are. That became Transit, the US Navy's satellite navigation system, an ancestor of GPS.

sputnik-2-satellite.name: Sputnik 2 satellite
sputnik-2-satellite.description: A sealed, air-conditioned cabin for one dog, with instruments for radiation and sunlight. It stays attached to the rocket's core stage in orbit.
sputnik-2-satellite.historyNote: Sputnik 2's Geiger counter, built by Sergei Vernov's team in Moscow, recorded strange swings in its counts. The team blamed a small solar flare. In fact the satellite had been dipping in and out of the radiation belts, months before Explorer 1. Its highest point was over the southern hemisphere, and an Australian team picked up its signals but had no code to read them.

vostok-capsule.name: Vostok capsule
vostok-capsule.description: A steel sphere for the cosmonaut, joined to an equipment module with batteries, oxygen and a single retrorocket that can't be restarted.
vostok-capsule.historyNote: Why a ball? A sphere whose weight sits slightly off-center settles heat-shield-first into the air on its own, like a weighted toy that rights itself. So Vostok needed no thrusters to hold its attitude during reentry. The price was a steep, uncontrolled descent: cosmonauts felt around eight times their own weight on the way down.

explorer-1-satellite.name: Explorer 1 satellite
explorer-1-satellite.description: A slim cylinder of about 14 kg carrying a Geiger counter, temperature sensors and a micrometeorite detector.
explorer-1-satellite.historyNote: Explorer 1 was meant to spin like a bullet around its long axis. After its first orbit it was tumbling end over end instead. Its flexing wire antennas were bleeding off energy, and a spinning body that loses energy drifts toward spinning around its fattest axis. The surprise taught engineers a rule that every spacecraft designer has followed since.

mercury-capsule.name: Mercury capsule
mercury-capsule.description: A small cone for one astronaut, with an escape tower on top, a heat shield at the base and a pack of retrorockets strapped over it.
mercury-capsule.historyNote: The first Mercury capsules had two small portholes and a side hatch held by 70 bolts, and the astronaut was meant to climb out through the nose. The astronauts pushed for a real window above their heads and a hatch they could blow off with explosive charges. Both arrived with Liberty Bell 7, the second crewed capsule.

r7-sputnik.name: R-7 (Sputnik)
r7-sputnik.description: The world's first intercontinental missile, adapted to carry a satellite: a core stage ringed by four strap-on boosters, all lit on the launch pad.
r7-sputnik.historyNote: Why light every engine on the ground? In the early 1950s nobody knew whether a large rocket engine could be started reliably high up, in thin air or in vacuum. The R-7's designers sidestepped the question: the core and all four boosters ignite on the pad, and the empty boosters simply fall away. Its descendant, Soyuz, still flies this way.

r7-vostok.name: R-7 (Vostok)
r7-vostok.description: The R-7 with a small upper stage on top, enough to put a crewed Vostok capsule into orbit.
r7-vostok.historyNote: Gagarin's rocket was the R-7 with a third stage, the Block E. Semyon Kosberg's bureau, which had built engines for aircraft, developed its engine in about nine months for the first Moon probes. Three of the first lunar launches failed, and on 2 January 1959 the stage worked for the first time, sending Luna 1 past the Moon. Gagarin rode an improved version of it.

jupiter-c.name: Jupiter-C
jupiter-c.description: A lengthened Redstone missile topped with a spinning cluster of small solid rockets, just enough to put a very light satellite into orbit.
jupiter-c.historyNote: In September 1956 this rocket could have put a satellite in orbit, a year before Sputnik. Washington wanted the first American satellite to come from the civilian Vanguard project, so the Army flew with a dummy top stage filled with sand, and the payload only arced 5,300 km downrange. After Sputnik and a Vanguard exploding on its pad, a Jupiter-C finally launched Explorer 1 in January 1958.

redstone.name: Redstone
redstone.description: A single-stage missile, made safe enough to carry an astronaut. It can only lob a capsule on a short suborbital hop.
redstone.historyNote: Mercury-Redstone 1, in November 1960, became known as the "four-inch flight": the rocket rose about ten centimeters and shut itself down, because a plug had come out in the wrong order and told it the flight was over. The capsule then fired its escape tower away on its own and released its parachutes, leaving a fully fueled rocket on the pad with parachutes draped down its side.

atlas.name: Atlas
atlas.description: A missile built so light that it needs the pressure in its tanks to keep its shape, and powerful enough to put a Mercury capsule into orbit.
atlas.historyNote: The Atlas's steel skin was thinner than a coin, so the rocket had to stay pressurized even on the ground, or it would buckle under its own weight. Like the R-7, it lit all its engines at liftoff, because nobody was sure an engine would start in space. Partway up it simply dropped its two outer engines and flew on with the one in the middle.

pegasus-satellite.name: Pegasus satellite
pegasus-satellite.description: Two long wings of thin detector panels that unfold in orbit, each panel recording the hits of tiny particles.
pegasus-satellite.historyNote: Pegasus answered a question Apollo's designers couldn't answer on the ground: how often would tiny meteoroids punch through a thin spacecraft skin? Its detector panels, and sample shields mounted on them, found far fewer penetrating hits than the worst fears. Engineers could trust the thin-skinned service module and the heat-shield cocoon of the command module.

biosatellite-satellite.name: Biosatellite capsule
biosatellite-satellite.description: A capsule with life support for its small passengers, and a heat shield and parachute to bring them home for study.
biosatellite-satellite.historyNote: Biosatellite 1 carried more than ten million small living things into orbit in December 1966: insects, frog eggs, bacteria, plants. Its capsule separated on schedule, but its small deorbit rocket never fired. The capsule stayed in orbit with its specimens and its data, and it was never recovered.

ofo-satellite.name: OFO satellite
ofo-satellite.description: A small satellite with a water-filled centrifuge for two frogs, wired to record their balance organs.
ofo-satellite.historyNote: The Orbiting Frog Otolith flew bullfrogs because their balance organs are very like ours. Fine electrodes recorded single nerve fibers from the inner-ear sensors that feel gravity, and the frogs rode in water, which cushioned them from the launch. The satellite was built to keep every acceleration below a thousandth of the Earth's gravity.

pioneer-4-probe.name: Pioneer 4 probe
pioneer-4-probe.description: A light cone carrying radiation counters, spun for stability and fired on a path past the Moon.
pioneer-4-probe.historyNote: Pioneer 4 weighed about 6 kg: a cone of fiberglass half a meter tall, washed with gold so it would conduct electricity and act as part of the antenna. The white stripes painted on it were its whole thermal control, meant to keep the inside between 10 and 50 degrees Celsius. A ring of mercury batteries powered it.

zond-5-probe.name: Zond 5 spacecraft
zond-5-probe.description: An uncrewed Soyuz 7K-L1 with a descent capsule and life support for its animal passengers.
zond-5-probe.historyNote: Zond 5's trip home went wrong. Its star tracker, fogged by gas from its own heated interior coating, delayed a course correction, and on the way back the capsule could not fly its planned guided reentry. It fell ballistically, at much higher g-forces than planned, into the Indian Ocean instead of Kazakhstan. The tortoises inside survived.

ranger-3-probe.name: Ranger 3 probe
ranger-3-probe.description: A probe with a television camera and a capsule meant to survive the impact and keep reporting.
ranger-3-probe.historyNote: Rangers 3 to 6 were baked before launch to kill any Earth microbes that might contaminate the Moon. The engineer running the sterilization warned that the heat was damaging the electronics, and NASA's board of inquiry agreed after the failures. Later Rangers were built with parts that were never baked, and Ranger 7 sent back over 4,000 pictures in 1964.

luna-2-probe.name: Luna 2 probe
luna-2-probe.description: A sphere of instruments and pennants bearing the Soviet emblem, built to strike the Moon.
luna-2-probe.historyNote: Luna 2 hit the Moon on 13 September 1959, the first human-made object to reach another world. It carried two balls covered in small metal pentagons engraved with the Soviet emblem, built to burst apart on impact and scatter them. Khrushchev gave a copy to President Eisenhower on his visit to the United States days later.

pioneer-2-probe.name: Pioneer 2 probe
pioneer-2-probe.description: A small probe with a kick motor of its own to brake into lunar orbit.
pioneer-2-probe.historyNote: Pioneer 1 and 2 were short cylinders with a cone at each end, built around a solid rocket that was meant to brake them into orbit around the Moon. Eight small rockets on the upper cone would trim their speed on the way. Each carried a scanning infrared camera, meant to take crude pictures of the Moon's surface.

lunar-orbiter-probe.name: Lunar Orbiter spacecraft
lunar-orbiter-probe.description: A camera with a small film laboratory on board, solar panels, and an engine for lunar orbit.
lunar-orbiter-probe.historyNote: On 23 August 1966 Lunar Orbiter 1 pointed its camera past the Moon's edge and photographed the Earth from about 380,000 km, the first picture of our planet from near the Moon. It wasn't on the plan: a fault in the camera's motion compensation had changed the film schedule and left room for a few unplanned frames.

surveyor-lander.name: Surveyor lander
surveyor-lander.description: A three-legged lander with a braking rocket, throttleable engines for the last stretch, and a camera.
surveyor-lander.historyNote: On 17 November 1967 Surveyor 6 fired its engines again on the Moon, rose about 4 meters and set down about 2.5 meters away: the first liftoff from another world. The hop let its camera look at its first landing site and judge the soil from a second angle, and it showed that a craft could fire its engines on the Moon.

luna-15-probe.name: Luna 15 lander
luna-15-probe.description: A landing stage with a drill arm, and a small ascent rocket carrying a sealed capsule for the sample.
luna-15-probe.historyNote: The Soviet sample-return craft needed no rendezvous and no navigator. After the drill had sealed its core in a small capsule, the ascent stage fired straight up from the lander and flew directly back toward Earth. Luna 16's capsule, in September 1970, plunged ballistically into the atmosphere and came down under a parachute in Kazakhstan.

luna-3-probe.name: Luna 3 probe
luna-3-probe.description: A probe with a camera that develops film on board and scans it for radio.
luna-3-probe.historyNote: Luna 3 spun slowly for most of its flight, but for its photographs it had to point. Photocells found the Sun and the Moon, small gas jets turned the craft and held it steady, and a photocell on its upper end started the camera when it saw the sunlit far side. It was the first Soviet spacecraft that could hold itself steady on all three axes.

luna-17-lander.name: Luna 17 lander
luna-17-lander.description: A landing stage with folding ramps at each end, for the rover to roll off.
luna-17-lander.historyNote: Luna 17's landing stage carried its rover on top, with folding ramps on two opposite sides, so Lunokhod could drive off whichever way was clear of boulders. It used the east side. The stage itself had a full rocket landing system of its own: a main engine, tanks and four legs, the same design that brought Luna 16's sample drill down two months earlier.

lunokhod-1-rover.name: Lunokhod rover
lunokhod-1-rover.description: An eight-wheeled rover under a hinged lid of solar cells, driven from Earth with a few seconds' delay.
lunokhod-1-rover.historyNote: Lunokhod 1 carried a French laser reflector. After the rover fell silent in 1971 nobody knew exactly where it had stopped, and laser beams from Earth found nothing for almost 40 years. In 2010 a NASA orbiter photographed the rover, and within weeks a telescope in New Mexico got a strong reflection back from it on its first try.

pioneer-6-probe.name: Pioneer Sun probe
pioneer-6-probe.description: A small drum-shaped probe covered in solar cells, spinning slowly to keep stable.
pioneer-6-probe.historyNote: Pioneer 6 and its three sisters, spaced around the Sun along the Earth's orbit, became the first solar weather network in space. They could see parts of the Sun days before its rotation turned them toward the Earth, and their warnings of solar storms went to airlines, power companies and NASA's planners for the Apollo flights.

mariner-10-probe.name: Mariner 10 probe
mariner-10-probe.description: A probe with two television cameras and a sunshade, steered past Venus and on to Mercury.
mariner-10-probe.historyNote: Mariner 10 was the first spacecraft to steer with the pressure of sunlight. Its gyroscopes and solar panels had set it wobbling, wasting the nitrogen gas its thrusters needed, so controllers tilted the two panels slightly differently and let sunlight pushing on them hold it steady. The gas ran out on 24 March 1975, eight days after its last pass of Mercury.

mariner-5-probe.name: Mariner 5 probe
mariner-5-probe.description: A flyby probe with instruments that read Venus's atmosphere from the way its radio signal bends.
mariner-5-probe.historyNote: Mariner 5 began as the spare for Mariner 4, the first probe to photograph Mars. When Mariner 4 worked, NASA rebuilt the spare for Venus: it lost its camera, gained a sunshade, and had its solar panels turned to face the other way and made smaller, since it would be flying toward the Sun instead of away.

pioneer-venus-orbiter-probe.name: Pioneer Venus Orbiter
pioneer-venus-orbiter-probe.description: A drum-shaped orbiter with a radar mapper and instruments for the upper atmosphere.
pioneer-venus-orbiter-probe.historyNote: Pioneer Venus 1 found a second career as a comet observatory. In early 1986, when Halley's Comet passed behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, the orbiter at Venus had a clear view. Its ultraviolet spectrometer tracked the hydrogen streaming off the comet and measured how much water it was losing, near the comet's most active time.

pioneer-venus-multiprobe-craft.name: Pioneer Venus Multiprobe
pioneer-venus-multiprobe-craft.description: A carrier bus with one large and three small entry probes, each with its own heat shield.
pioneer-venus-multiprobe-craft.historyNote: The bus that carried the four Pioneer Venus probes had no heat shield and no parachute, but it was not wasted. About 90 minutes after the probes went in, it followed them, and its two mass spectrometers sampled the thin upper air that the probes had fallen through too fast to measure. It sent data for about a minute before it burned up near 110 km.

venera-15-probe.name: Venera 15 orbiter
venera-15-probe.description: An orbiter carrying a large dish for side-looking radar mapping.
venera-15-probe.historyNote: Venera 15 and 16 were built from the orbiter half of the earlier Venera lander missions, with a radar dish about 6 meters long in place of a lander. Because Venus is hidden under its clouds, they mapped it by radar from the side, at a resolution of one to two kilometers, over eight months.

venera-7-probe.name: Venera 7 lander
venera-7-probe.description: A small, heavily insulated descent capsule built to withstand Venus's pressure and heat.
venera-7-probe.historyNote: Venera 4 had been built for about 10 atmospheres of pressure and was crushed high above the ground; Venera 5 and 6 were built for 25 and crushed too. Venera 7's lander was built for 180 atmospheres and 540 degrees Celsius, with a titanium hull in place of aluminum and magnesium alloy, and was chilled to about −8 °C by its carrier before entry. The extra strength cost weight, so it carried few instruments.

venera-9-probe.name: Venera lander and carrier
venera-9-probe.description: A carrier that can fly past or orbit Venus, and a lander protected by a spherical shell.
venera-9-probe.historyNote: Venera 9's lander dropped its parachutes about 50 km above Venus, while it was still far from the ground. Below that the air is so thick that a flat metal disc around the lander, about 2 meters across, was brake enough: it came down the rest of the way on the disc alone and touched the ground at about 7 meters per second.

mariner-6-probe.name: Mariner 6 probe
mariner-6-probe.description: A flyby probe with cameras and spectrometers on a turntable platform.
mariner-6-probe.historyNote: Mariner 4 had sent its pictures of Mars home at about 8 bits a second; each picture took hours. Mariner 6 and 7 had a channel for 16,200 bits a second, almost 2,000 times as fast. Together they sent back about 200 pictures in 1969, against Mariner 4's 22 four years earlier.

mariner-9-probe.name: Mariner 9 orbiter
mariner-9-probe.description: An orbiter with a large engine for braking into Mars orbit, and cameras for mapping.
mariner-9-probe.historyNote: Mariner 9 had a twin. Mariner 8 was launched on 8 May 1971, but its Centaur upper stage began to tumble and it fell into the Atlantic. Mariner 9 left three weeks later with a repaired Centaur and both missions' work in its plan: mapping most of the planet, and watching how its surface and air changed over time.

viking-orbiter.name: Viking orbiter
viking-orbiter.description: An orbiter that carries the lander to Mars, scouts its landing site and relays its signals.
viking-orbiter.historyNote: On 25 July 1976, while it was looking for a landing site for Viking 2, the Viking 1 orbiter photographed a hill in the Cydonia region that looked like a human face, with the Sun low and the shadows making eyes, a nose and a mouth. NASA released it as a curiosity. Higher-resolution pictures in 1998 showed an ordinary eroded hill.

viking-lander.name: Viking lander
viking-lander.description: A lander with a sampling arm and a small onboard laboratory to look for signs of life.
viking-lander.historyNote: To keep Earth's microbes off Mars, each Viking lander was sealed in a protective shell and baked whole at about 112 degrees Celsius for some 40 hours, with every part designed to survive it. The shell stayed closed until the spacecraft had left Earth orbit. It was one of the most thorough sterilizations of any spacecraft.

mars-2-probe.name: Mars 2 spacecraft
mars-2-probe.description: An orbiter with a lander attached, the lander carrying a small rover tethered by a cable.
mars-2-probe.historyNote: Mars 2 and 3 arrived during the biggest dust storm ever seen on Mars, but they could not wait: their computers released the landers on a schedule set before launch, and it couldn't be changed. Mariner 9, arriving at the same time, simply waited in orbit. The Mars 2 lander crashed on 27 November 1971, the first human-made object to reach the surface.

mars-m69-probe.name: Mars M-69 orbiter
mars-m69-probe.description: A heavy orbiter with cameras, built to make full use of the Proton's lift.
mars-m69-probe.historyNote: The M-69 orbiters weighed about 4.85 tonnes, far more than earlier Soviet planetary probes, and needed the new Proton rocket. Georgy Babakin's team at Lavochkin threw out the planned design and started a new spacecraft only 13 months before launch. Both were lost when their Protons failed, one in the third stage and one about 30 seconds after liftoff.

pioneer-10-probe.name: Pioneer 10 probe
pioneer-10-probe.description: A probe powered by radioisotope generators, since sunlight is too weak at Jupiter for solar panels.
pioneer-10-probe.historyNote: Sunlight at Jupiter is too weak for solar panels of any practical size, so Pioneer 10 carried four small nuclear generators that turned the heat of decaying plutonium into about 155 watts. They rode on two 3-meter trusses to keep them well away from the instruments, and a third boom held the magnetometer more than 6 meters out.

pioneer-11-probe.name: Pioneer 11 probe
pioneer-11-probe.description: A twin of Pioneer 10, steered through Jupiter's gravity onto a path to Saturn.
pioneer-11-probe.historyNote: At Saturn in September 1979, Pioneer 11 crossed the plane of the rings at the same distance Voyager 2 would have to cross it to go on to Uranus. If the faint outer region held enough ring material to wreck a spacecraft, better to find out with Pioneer. It got through safely, found a new ring, now the F ring, and nearly hit a small, unknown moon.

agena-target-vehicle.name: Agena target vehicle
agena-target-vehicle.description: An upper stage with a docking collar and an engine that can restart: a target for docking practice, and once docked, a stage that can push the capsule higher.
agena-target-vehicle.historyNote: On 25 October 1965 Gemini 6's crew sat on the pad waiting for their Agena to reach orbit. It exploded about six minutes after launch, and the flight was scrubbed. Within days NASA had a new plan: launch Gemini 7 on its two-week flight, and use it as Gemini 6's target. In December the two capsules flew in formation, as close as about 30 centimeters.

x-15-aircraft.name: X-15 rocket plane
x-15-aircraft.description: A black, stubby-winged rocket plane with a single rocket engine and small thrusters for control where the air runs out.
x-15-aircraft.historyNote: Above about Mach 5 the air heats a plane's skin to hundreds of degrees, enough to ruin aluminum. The X-15's outer skin was Inconel X, a nickel-chrome alloy, and its structure was designed to soak up the heat of the short, fast flights like a sponge. The pilot sat in an aluminum cabin kept apart from the hot outer shell.

mig-e-154-spaceplane.name: MiG E-154 rocket plane
mig-e-154-spaceplane.description: A slender swept-wing rocket plane with a cluster of four rocket engines, a pressurized cockpit, wheels to land on and small thrusters for control above the air.
mig-e-154-spaceplane.historyNote: The real Soviet space plane project, Spiral, planned to launch its orbiter from the back of a hypersonic carrier aircraft: a 52-tonne jet that would climb to almost 30 km at up to six times the speed of sound before releasing it. The carrier was never built, but a subsonic test version of the orbiter flew eight times after being dropped from a Tu-95 bomber.

voskhod-capsule.name: Voskhod capsule
voskhod-capsule.description: A Vostok sphere with the ejection seat removed to fit more people, a backup retrorocket, and an inflatable airlock.
voskhod-capsule.historyNote: Voskhod was a Vostok with the ejection seat taken out and three couches squeezed in, set crosswise. There was no room for spacesuits, and no way out on the pad or during landing: the crew rode the capsule all the way down, so a small rocket on the parachute lines fired just before touchdown to soften the landing. The crew of Voskhod 1 said they barely felt it.

gemini-capsule.name: Gemini capsule
gemini-capsule.description: A two-person capsule with thrusters to change orbit, a radar for rendezvous, and a nose that can dock.
gemini-capsule.historyNote: Gemini was the first crewed spacecraft with a digital computer on board, built by IBM: about 27 kg with 4,096 words of core memory. It worked out the burns for rendezvous, steered during reentry, and stood by as a backup for the Titan rocket's guidance. Mercury had none: its pilots flew with the ground doing the arithmetic.

gemini-transtage.name: Gemini Transtage
gemini-transtage.description: The Titan's restartable upper stage, docked to a Gemini in orbit to push it toward the Moon.
gemini-transtage.historyNote: The Transtage was the restartable top stage of the Titan III, burning fuels that light on contact so it could be fired again and again. On 16 June 1966 a Titan IIIC used it to place seven small military communications satellites, and a test satellite, into high orbit on a single launch. McDonnell's Moon proposals would have docked a Gemini to one to push it out of Earth orbit.

gemini-lunar-propulsion-module.name: Gemini lunar propulsion module
gemini-lunar-propulsion-module.description: A propulsion module behind the capsule, with enough engine to brake into lunar orbit and leave again.
gemini-lunar-propulsion-module.historyNote: Coming home from the Moon means hitting the air at about 11 km/s instead of about 7.8 from Earth orbit, with far more heating. That doomed the simplest lunar Gemini plan: a Centaur stage on a Titan II, good for a 72-hour flight around the Moon, was quickly dropped over worries about Gemini's heat shield. Any lunar Gemini would have needed a new one.

gemini-direct-ascent-craft.name: Gemini Direct Ascent spacecraft
gemini-direct-ascent-craft.description: A Gemini capsule stacked on landing and ascent modules, all landing on the Moon together.
gemini-direct-ascent-craft.historyNote: McDonnell's direct-ascent Gemini would have braked toward the Moon with a module built around the RL10, the hydrogen-burning engine of the Centaur stage. The RL10 first flew on 27 November 1963, the first hydrogen engine to fire in space. Versions of it are still flying today, on upper stages of rockets that launch satellites and probes.

gemini-eor-service-module.name: Gemini EOR service module
gemini-eor-service-module.description: A service module for the lunar trip, joined to the capsule in Earth orbit.
gemini-eor-service-module.historyNote: Gemini's real service section stayed in orbit: everything that didn't need to come home, the thrusters, the propellant, the oxygen, the power, was packed in an adapter behind the capsule and discarded before reentry. Gemini 5 in 1965 was the first to carry fuel cells there, making electricity from hydrogen and oxygen, with water as the byproduct, for an eight-day flight.

langley-lunar-lander.name: Langley light lunar lander
langley-lunar-lander.description: A minimal open lander for one astronaut in a spacesuit: little more than an engine, tanks and a seat.
langley-lunar-lander.historyNote: NASA Langley's lander idea of 1961 was never built, but Langley built the next best thing: a steel gantry about 70 meters tall that held up five-sixths of a full-size lander's weight on cables. Twenty-four Apollo astronauts practiced the last 150 feet of a lunar landing there. Asked what landing on the Moon was like, Neil Armstrong said: like Langley.

s-ivb-space-tug.name: S-IVB Space Tug
s-ivb-space-tug.description: A Saturn upper stage used as a tug in Earth orbit, pushing the assembled craft out toward the Moon.
s-ivb-space-tug.historyNote: From Apollo 13 on, the spent S-IVB stage wasn't sent off into orbit around the Sun but steered into the Moon. Apollo 13's stage hit at about 2.6 km/s on 15 April 1970, about 135 km from the seismometer Apollo 12 had left behind. The shaking it recorded helped work out what lies under the Moon's surface. Its crater is about 30 meters across.

apollo-csm.name: Apollo command and service module
apollo-csm.description: The three-person command module and the service module behind it, whose engine brakes into lunar orbit and brings the crew home.
apollo-csm.historyNote: The engine that brought Apollo home from the Moon had to work. So it was as simple as an engine can be: fed by gas pressure instead of pumps, with fuel and oxidizer that ignite on contact, so it needed no igniter. Its valves, plumbing and electronics were doubled; only the combustion chamber and nozzle had no backup.

apollo-lunar-module.name: Apollo lunar module
apollo-lunar-module.description: A two-stage lander: the descent stage stays on the Moon as a launch pad, the ascent stage flies the crew back to orbit.
apollo-lunar-module.historyNote: Grumman fought the lunar module's weight from the first drawing. The seats went, so the crew flew standing, held by harnesses, which let the windows shrink because the astronauts' eyes were closer to them. In places the pressurized cabin's wall was about 0.3 mm thick, a few layers of kitchen foil, wrapped in insulation and a thin outer skin.

soyuz-7k-l1-spacecraft.name: Soyuz 7K-L1 spacecraft
soyuz-7k-l1-spacecraft.description: A Soyuz without its orbital module, to save weight for the trip around the Moon.
soyuz-7k-l1-spacecraft.historyNote: On its way back from the Moon in November 1968, Zond 6 lost its cabin air through a faulty seal, and its parachute was released too high. It crashed in Kazakhstan, and engineers had to dig its film out of the wreck; the far-side photographs were published anyway. A crew aboard would not have survived, and Apollo 8 flew around the Moon the next month.

soyuz-7k-lok-spacecraft.name: Soyuz 7K-LOK spacecraft
soyuz-7k-lok-spacecraft.description: A Soyuz built for lunar orbit, with a bigger engine and a docking system for the LK lander.
soyuz-7k-lok-spacecraft.historyNote: The lunar Soyuz, the 7K-LOK, flew only on top of an N1. On 23 November 1972 the fourth N1 lifted off with an uncrewed LOK and a dummy LK aboard for a test around the Moon. After 107 seconds, just before its first stage was due to finish, an engine exploded. The launch escape system pulled the spacecraft clear. It was the last N1 ever launched.

lk-lander.name: LK lander
lk-lander.description: A one-person lunar lander whose own engine block both finishes the landing and lifts it off again.
lk-lander.historyNote: Apollo's lunar module had two stages, one to land and one to take off. The LK used the same rocket unit for both, with a main engine and a backup beside it, because a failure on liftoff would strand the cosmonaut for good. A separate braking stage did most of the slowing and dropped away about 4 km above the surface.

soyuz-7k-ok-spacecraft.name: Soyuz 7K-OK spacecraft
soyuz-7k-ok-spacecraft.description: The Earth-orbit Soyuz: a descent module, an orbital module for living space, and a service module.
soyuz-7k-ok-spacecraft.historyNote: Vostok's ball fell through the air ballistically, with eight g or more on the pilot. Soyuz's bell-shaped descent capsule carries its weight off-center, so it flies tilted and makes a little lift, and turning it steers the landing and spreads the braking over a longer path: about four g on a normal return. In an emergency it spins to cancel the lift and falls straight in, at higher g.

igla-docking-system.name: Igla docking system
igla-docking-system.description: Radar antennas and electronics that let two Soyuz craft find each other and dock with nobody steering.
igla-docking-system.historyNote: Igla, Russian for needle, measured direction and distance to its target by comparing radio signals across several antennas. It needed the target to help: the station or craft being approached had to turn its docking port toward the newcomer and keep it there. For large stations that cost too much fuel, so in the 1980s Igla gave way to Kurs.

lk-700-spacecraft.name: LK-700 spacecraft
lk-700-spacecraft.description: A heavy lunar craft built to land and take off again in one piece, with no rendezvous in lunar orbit.
lk-700-spacecraft.historyNote: The LK-700 grew out of Vladimir Chelomei's LK-1, a two-seat craft for flying around the Moon on his Proton rocket. In 1965 the government took the flyby from him and gave it to Korolev, whose Soyuz 7K-L1 flew instead. Chelomei turned to landing, and presented the direct-ascent LK-700 to an expert commission in November 1966.

gemini-eva-suit.name: Gemini spacesuit
gemini-eva-suit.description: A pressure suit with an umbilical hose for oxygen and a tether, for work outside the capsule.
gemini-eva-suit.historyNote: On Gemini 9A in June 1966 Gene Cernan was to strap on a rocket backpack at the rear of the spacecraft. With nothing to brace against, every move took far more effort than expected; his heart rate climbed to about 180 and his breath fogged his visor from the inside. The backpack test was called off. Better cooling, foot restraints, handholds and underwater training followed.

apollo-lunar-eva-suit.name: Apollo lunar surface suit
apollo-lunar-eva-suit.description: A suit with its own backpack for oxygen and cooling, built for hours of walking on the Moon.
apollo-lunar-eva-suit.historyNote: Apollo's moon suits came from ILC, the company behind Playtex bras and girdles, and the women who sewed them came from its Playtex sewing floor. Each suit was made by hand to fit one astronaut, from about 21 layers, some glued and some stitched, with seams that had to be accurate to the width of a pin.

light-lunar-eva-suit.name: Light lunar suit
light-lunar-eva-suit.description: A lighter surface suit for the open Langley lander, where the suit is the crew's only cabin.
light-lunar-eva-suit.historyNote: How do you cool an astronaut in a vacuum? Apollo's life-support backpack pumped cold water through tubes in a garment worn under the suit, then past a metal plate full of tiny pores with vacuum on the far side. Water seeping through the plate froze, and the ice turned straight to vapor, carrying the body's heat away. The more heat, the faster the ice went.

lunar-roving-vehicle.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle
lunar-roving-vehicle.description: A folding electric car for two astronauts, carried on the lunar module's side.
lunar-roving-vehicle.historyNote: On Apollo 17's first moonwalk Gene Cernan caught a rover fender with a hammer and tore part of it off, and the wheels began throwing up plumes of dark dust. Overnight, engineers on the ground worked out a fix: next morning the crew taped four spare maps together into a new fender and fixed it in place with two clamps borrowed from the lunar module's lights.

berkut-eva-suit.name: Berkut spacesuit
berkut-eva-suit.description: A Soviet pressure suit with a backpack of oxygen, made for the first walk outside a spacecraft.
berkut-eva-suit.historyNote: Leonov's Berkut suit was white rather than the orange of earlier Soviet suits, so it would reflect sunlight, and it carried 30 to 45 minutes of oxygen in a backpack. It ran at 0.4 atmospheres, a compromise between enough pressure to breathe and a suit soft enough to bend.

yastreb-eva-suit.name: Yastreb spacesuit
yastreb-eva-suit.description: A suit for spacewalks between two docked Soyuz craft.
yastreb-eva-suit.historyNote: The Yastreb carried its life support in a white metal box on the chest and stomach rather than on the back, so it would fit through Soyuz's narrow hatches. Two cosmonauts wore it in January 1969 to cross from Soyuz 5 to Soyuz 4 on the outside. Nobody filmed the crossing: the camera that was meant to record it was never set up.

krechet-eva-suit.name: Krechet lunar suit
krechet-eva-suit.description: A semi-rigid lunar suit entered through a hatch in its back.
krechet-eva-suit.historyNote: A cosmonaut landing alone on the Moon would have nobody to help with the zips. So the Krechet lunar suit was entered through a door in its back, with the backpack built into the door, and closed with a lever by the right elbow. The idea outlived the Moon program: the Orlan suits Russian cosmonauts still use for spacewalks open the same way.

r7-voskhod.name: R-7 (Voskhod)
r7-voskhod.description: The R-7 with a more powerful upper stage, able to lift the heavier Voskhod.
r7-voskhod.historyNote: The Voskhod rocket, the R-7 with a bigger third stage, flew about 300 times between 1963 and 1976. Only two of those launches carried people. Many of the rest put Zenit reconnaissance satellites into orbit, spy satellites whose cameras and film came back to Earth in a capsule. Its busiest year, 1969, saw 32 flights.

r7-luna.name: R-7 (Luna)
r7-luna.description: The R-7 with a small third stage that sends probes to the Moon.
r7-luna.historyNote: Luna 1 left on 2 January 1959, on the first R-7 with a third stage that worked. The next day, about 113,000 km out, it released a kilogram of sodium vapor, a glowing artificial comet that observers photographed from the ground to check its path. It was aimed at the Moon, missed by about 6,000 km because of an error in the engine's cutoff, and became the first spacecraft to orbit the Sun.

r7-molniya.name: R-7 (Molniya)
r7-molniya.description: The R-7 with a stage that restarts in orbit, for flights to the Moon and the planets.
r7-molniya.historyNote: The R-7 with a fourth stage was named after its most famous payload: Molniya, Russian for lightning, the first Soviet communications satellites. They flew a long 12-hour orbit tilted at 63.4 degrees, at which the orbit's high point doesn't drift. Each satellite hung for hours high over the far north, where satellites over the equator are hard to see from, and three of them covered it around the clock.

r7-soyuz.name: R-7 (Soyuz)
r7-soyuz.description: The R-7 version built for the Soyuz spacecraft, with an escape tower for the crew.
r7-soyuz.historyNote: The R-7 began as the world's first intercontinental missile in the 1950s, and it was soon too big and slow to be a good one. As a launcher it never retired: its Soyuz descendants still carry crews into orbit today. Counting every version, the family has flown more than 1,900 times, more than any other rocket in history.

proton.name: Proton
proton.description: A heavy rocket on storable propellants, powerful enough for the largest probes.
proton.historyNote: Vladimir Chelomei designed the UR-500 as a missile to carry an enormous nuclear warhead. It never served as one. Its first flights, from July 1965, carried Proton, a series of heavy satellites of over 12 tonnes for studying cosmic rays, and the rocket took their name. Modern versions of it were still flying more than half a century later.

proton-k-block-d.name: Proton-K with Block D
proton-k-block-d.description: The Proton with a restartable upper stage, able to send a crewed craft around the Moon.
proton-k-block-d.historyNote: The Block D stage was built for the Soviet Moon landing: as the N1's fifth stage it would correct the course to the Moon, brake into lunar orbit and start the LK's descent. On top of a Proton it found a longer life, sending Zond capsules around the Moon, and Luna 16, Lunokhod, Mars 3 and Venera 9 on their way. A later version first took Soviet satellites to geostationary orbit.

n1.name: N1
n1.description: The giant Soviet Moon rocket, its first stage driven by a ring of many smaller engines.
n1.historyNote: The N1's first stage had 30 engines, more than any rocket before it. A control system called KORD watched them, and if one failed it shut down the one opposite to keep the thrust balanced. All four launches failed. On the second, on 3 July 1969, an oxygen pump exploded as it lifted off, and the rocket fell back onto the pad, and the pad took about 18 months to rebuild.

ur-700.name: UR-700
ur-700.description: A proposed giant rocket for a direct flight to the Moon, built from storable-propellant modules.
ur-700.historyNote: Chelomei's UR-700 was a bundle of rocket modules with one big engine each: six around the outside as the first stage and three in the middle as the second, nine engines in all, carrying about 150 tonnes to low orbit. Its RD-270 engine, by Valentin Glushko's bureau, was test-fired 27 times between 1967 and 1969, but the rocket was never built.

juno-2.name: Juno II
juno-2.description: A Jupiter missile with small solid upper stages, for probes to the Moon and beyond.
juno-2.historyNote: The Juno II was a Jupiter missile with stretched tanks, a stronger frame for the upper stages and radio guidance from the ground, topped with clusters of small solid rockets. It had a rough record: six of its ten launches failed. Pioneer 4 in March 1959 was a success, and so was Explorer 7 in October 1959, which made the first measurements of the energy the Earth gains from the Sun and gives off.

thor-able.name: Thor-Able
thor-able.description: A Thor missile with an upper stage on top: an early workhorse for small satellites and probes.
thor-able.historyNote: On 14 August 1959 Explorer 6, launched a week earlier on a Thor-Able, sent back the first picture of the Earth from orbit. Its camera was a simple scanning eye that swept the view in strips as the satellite spun, and engineers pieced the strips together like a shredded letter. The blurry result showed sunlit clouds over the Pacific, the first step toward weather satellites.

atlas-agena.name: Atlas-Agena
atlas-agena.description: An Atlas with the restartable Agena upper stage, for lunar and planetary probes.
atlas-agena.historyNote: On 22 July 1962 an Atlas-Agena carrying Mariner 1 to Venus veered off course and was destroyed. A symbol in the guidance equations had lost its bar, the mark meaning a smoothed average, so the software chased noise as if it were real drift. The press called it the most expensive hyphen in history. Five weeks later Mariner 2 left for Venus, and it made the first flyby of another planet in December.

atlas-centaur.name: Atlas-Centaur
atlas-centaur.description: An Atlas with the Centaur, the first upper stage burning liquid hydrogen, for heavier probes.
atlas-centaur.historyNote: The first Atlas-Centaur, in May 1962, broke up less than a minute after launch when insulation panels on the hydrogen tank failed. Wernher von Braun recommended cancelling the stage, and in November President Kennedy suggested the same. It survived because Surveyor depended on it, and because Apollo needed experience with liquid hydrogen. In 1966 it sent Surveyor 1 to its landing on the Moon.

titan-2.name: Titan II
titan-2.description: A missile on storable propellants, made human-rated to fly the Gemini capsule.
titan-2.historyNote: The Titan II was a missile, and it shook: a vibration along its length that the Air Force could live with was far beyond what NASA would accept for astronauts, a quarter of a g. A first fix made it worse, doubling the shaking. Then engineers found the cause, bubbles forming at the pump inlets, and gas-filled dampers in the feed lines brought it down to about a tenth of a g.

titan-3c.name: Titan IIIC
titan-3c.description: A Titan with two large solid boosters strapped to its sides and a Transtage on top.
titan-3c.historyNote: The Titan IIIC lifted off on its two big solid boosters alone, each three meters wide and built from five segments stacked near the pad. The liquid-fuelled core in the middle only lit high in the air, as the solids' thrust tailed off. At its first flight in 1965 it was the most powerful rocket that had ever flown.

titan-3e-centaur.name: Titan IIIE-Centaur
titan-3e-centaur.description: A Titan with solid boosters and a Centaur on top, for the outer planets.
titan-3e-centaur.historyNote: The first Titan IIIE-Centaur, in February 1974, failed when its Centaur stage did not ignite. It flew six more times and never failed again, and those six flights launched some of the most famous probes there are: Helios 1 and 2 toward the Sun, Viking 1 and 2 to Mars, and Voyager 2 and Voyager 1 to the outer planets.

saturn-1.name: Saturn I
saturn-1.description: The first Saturn, its first stage a cluster of eight engines fed from a cluster of tanks.
saturn-1.historyNote: The Saturn I's first stage was a bundle: eight narrow tanks around one wide one, all at the diameters of the Redstone and Jupiter missiles so their tooling could be used, feeding eight engines. Skeptics called it Cluster's Last Stand. It flew ten times without a failure, launched the three Pegasus satellites and flew test versions of the Apollo spacecraft.

saturn-1b.name: Saturn IB
saturn-1b.description: An improved Saturn I with a hydrogen upper stage, able to put an Apollo into Earth orbit.
saturn-1b.historyNote: The Saturn IB was much shorter than the Saturn V, but the launch pads at the Kennedy Space Center had been built for the giant. So NASA stood it on a pedestal about 39 meters tall, nicknamed the milkstool, until its upper stage and spacecraft lined up with the service arms. It launched the three Skylab crews from it in 1973.

saturn-c3b.name: Saturn C-3B
saturn-c3b.description: A Saturn design between the IB and the V, for lunar missions assembled in Earth orbit.
saturn-c3b.historyNote: The C in the early Saturn names wasn't an abbreviation: the designs were options lettered A, B and C, and Saturn C was chosen and numbered. The C-1 became the Saturn I and the C-5 the Saturn V. The C-3 never flew: it would have used two of the Saturn V's big engines, and Marshall planned to build a Moon ship from several of them in Earth orbit.

saturn-v.name: Saturn V
saturn-v.description: The three-stage giant that sends a complete Apollo spacecraft to the Moon.
saturn-v.historyNote: The Saturn V's F-1 engines suffered from combustion instability: pressure waves sloshing across the combustion chamber could tear an engine apart within moments. Engineers added copper baffles across the injector plate, then tested them the hard way, setting off small bombs inside running engines to see whether the baffles would calm the disturbance. It took more than 1,300 test firings.

sputnik-1-orbit.name: Orbital flight
sputnik-1-orbit.description: Launch the satellite and keep it transmitting from orbit for a season.

sputnik-1-extended.name: Extended mission
sputnik-1-extended.description: A longer flight with more battery capacity, spread over three seasons, for more science and more prestige. Sputnik 1 never flew one: this is what a next step could have looked like.

sputnik-2-orbit.name: Orbital flight with a dog
sputnik-2-orbit.description: Put the cabin and its passenger into orbit and send back the dog's heartbeat and breathing. There is no return.

korabl-sputnik-2-orbit.name: Biological flight and recovery
korabl-sputnik-2-orbit.description: A day in orbit with a cabin full of animals and plants, then retrofire, reentry and a landing on home territory with everything alive.

11-descent-and-splashdown.name: Descent and landing
11-descent-and-splashdown.description: Parachutes bring the capsule down on home territory, where the recovery team gets the animals out and back to the doctors.

vostok-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
vostok-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Try out the capsule on a short up-and-down flight, with a mannequin in the seat, before risking a pilot. The real program skipped this step: the R-7 was built for orbit.

08-retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire anyway, to test them for the orbital flights to come. On a suborbital arc the craft comes down whether they work or not.

10-reentry.description: Falling back steeply into the atmosphere: much slower than coming down from orbit, but hard enough to brake at around ten times normal weight.

vostok-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
vostok-suborbital.description: A pilot's first ride: about a quarter of an hour on a ballistic arc with a few minutes of weightlessness, then an ejection and a parachute landing.

07-retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire anyway, to test them for the orbital flights to come. On a suborbital arc the craft comes down whether they work or not.

10-reentry.description: Falling back steeply into the atmosphere: much slower than coming down from orbit, but hard enough to brake at around ten times normal weight.

vostok-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
vostok-uncrewed-orbital.description: One full orbit with nobody aboard, flown by the automatics and brought down on command from the ground. A mannequin in the seat tests the ejection.
vostok-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: The 'pilot' of the last two test flights, in March 1961, was a mannequin called Ivan Ivanovich, the Russian 'John Doe'. To test the radio without starting rumors of a secret cosmonaut, his voice channel played a recording of a choir and of a man reading out a recipe for borscht.

vostok-orbital.name: Orbital flight
vostok-orbital.description: The real thing: a cosmonaut aboard for at least one full orbit, then retrofire, reentry and ejection over home ground.
vostok-orbital.historyNote: Nobody knew whether a person could still think clearly in weightlessness, so Vostok 1's manual controls were locked. The unlock code, 1-2-5, was sealed in an envelope on board, on the theory that anyone able to enter it was fit to fly. Several people simply told Gagarin the code before launch.

vostok-orbital-duration-1.name: Day-long orbital flight
vostok-orbital-duration-1.description: Stay up for a full day or more and show that a person can eat, sleep and work in weightlessness.
vostok-orbital-duration-1.historyNote: In August 1961 Gherman Titov spent just over a day in orbit on Vostok 2. He was the first person to sleep in space, and the first to suffer from space sickness, which worried the doctors enough to shape the following flights.

vostok-orbital-duration-2.name: Multi-day orbital flight
vostok-orbital-duration-2.description: Several days in orbit, as long as the capsule's supplies allow, with the cosmonaut's health watched the whole time.
vostok-orbital-duration-2.historyNote: Valery Bykovsky's Vostok 5, in June 1963, stayed up for almost five days. It is still the longest spaceflight anyone has made alone. Two days into his flight, Valentina Tereshkova launched on Vostok 6 and became the first woman in space.

vostok-joint-orbital.name: Group flight
