vostok-joint-orbital.description: Launch two capsules a day apart into almost the same orbit, so that they pass close enough to talk by radio.
vostok-joint-orbital.historyNote: In August 1962 Vostok 3 and 4 came within about 6.5 km of each other, and the press spoke of a rendezvous. It wasn't one: neither capsule could change its orbit, the second launch was simply timed perfectly, and the two drifted apart. Real rendezvous is counterintuitive: to catch a craft ahead of you, you first slow down, which drops you to a lower, faster orbit.

explorer-1-orbit.name: Orbital flight
explorer-1-orbit.description: Launch the satellite and send back what its instruments find, for a season.
explorer-1-orbit.historyNote: Explorer 1's Geiger counter kept going quiet at high altitude. James Van Allen's team worked out why: the radiation up there was so intense that it overwhelmed the counter. They had found belts of charged particles trapped by the Earth's magnetic field, now named after him: the first great scientific discovery of the space age.

explorer-1-extended.name: Extended mission
explorer-1-extended.description: A longer flight with more battery capacity, spread over three seasons, for more science and more prestige. Explorer 1 never flew one: this is what a next step could have looked like.

mercury-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
mercury-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the capsule on a short arc without an astronaut, to prove the rocket, the escape system and the recovery at sea.
mercury-uncrewed-suborbital.historyNote: In January 1961, ahead of Alan Shepard, a chimpanzee named Ham rode the capsule. He pulled levers in answer to lights during the flight, showing that work was possible in weightlessness. His capsule came down far off target and began taking on water before the recovery helicopter reached it.

07-retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire anyway, to test them for the orbital flights to come. On a suborbital arc the craft comes down whether they work or not.

10-reentry.description: Falling back steeply into the atmosphere: much slower than coming down from orbit, but hard enough to brake at around ten times normal weight.

mercury-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
mercury-suborbital.description: About fifteen minutes on a ballistic arc: launch, a few minutes of weightlessness, and a splashdown far downrange.
mercury-suborbital.historyNote: In July 1961, moments after splashdown, Liberty Bell 7's hatch blew off. Gus Grissom swam out as the capsule filled and sank. It lay on the floor of the Atlantic, nearly 5 km down, until an expedition raised it in 1999.

07-retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire anyway, to test them for the orbital flights to come. On a suborbital arc the craft comes down whether they work or not.

10-reentry.description: Falling back steeply into the atmosphere: much slower than coming down from orbit, but hard enough to brake at around ten times normal weight.

mercury-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
mercury-uncrewed-orbital.description: Send the capsule around the Earth with no astronaut aboard, to prove its life support and controls before risking a crew.
mercury-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: In November 1961 a chimpanzee named Enos flew two orbits in a Mercury capsule. The flight was cut short by a stuck thruster and an overheating suit system, problems that were fixed before John Glenn flew the same mission three months later.

mercury-orbital.name: Orbital flight
mercury-orbital.description: An astronaut aboard for a few orbits, then retrofire, reentry and splashdown where the recovery ships wait.
mercury-orbital.historyNote: Scott Carpenter's Aurora 7, in May 1962, came down about 400 km past its target. The capsule was misaligned when the retrorockets fired, and they fired a few seconds late. He waited in his life raft for about three hours before a helicopter lifted him out.

mercury-orbital-duration-1.name: Day-long orbital flight
mercury-orbital-duration-1.description: A day or more in orbit, to learn how a person copes with weightlessness over a whole day of work and sleep.
mercury-orbital-duration-1.historyNote: Gordon Cooper's Faith 7, in May 1963, flew 22 orbits in about 34 hours. Near the end, a short circuit knocked out the automatic controls. Cooper lined the capsule up using lines drawn on his window, timed the retrofire with his wristwatch, and flew the reentry by hand, splashing down a few kilometers from the recovery ship.

mercury-joint-orbital.name: Joint launch
mercury-joint-orbital.description: Two capsules launched close together into neighboring orbits. Mercury never flew this: it points toward the rendezvous flights that came next.

pegasus-orbit.name: Orbital flight
pegasus-orbit.description: Unfold the panels in orbit and count micrometeoroid hits for a season.

pegasus-extended.name: Extended mission
pegasus-extended.description: Keep counting impacts for several seasons, for a far better estimate of the risk.

biosatellite-orbit.name: Orbital flight
biosatellite-orbit.description: Fly the organisms in orbit and recover the capsule with them.

biosatellite-extended.name: Extended mission
biosatellite-extended.description: A longer stay in orbit before recovery, to see how the organisms develop over time.

orbiting-frog-otolith-orbit.name: Orbital flight
orbiting-frog-otolith-orbit.description: Record the frogs' balance organs as they adjust to weightlessness.

orbiting-frog-otolith-extended.name: Extended mission
orbiting-frog-otolith-extended.description: Keep recording for longer, to see whether the frogs' sense of balance settles.

pioneer-4-flyby.name: Lunar flyby
pioneer-4-flyby.description: Fly past the Moon, measuring radiation on the way, and on into orbit around the Sun.

zond-5-flyby.name: Lunar flyby with animals
zond-5-flyby.description: Send the uncrewed capsule around the Moon and bring its passengers home through the atmosphere at lunar return speed.

ranger-3-impact.name: Lunar impact
ranger-3-impact.description: Aim the probe at the Moon and send pictures until it strikes.

luna-2-impact.name: Lunar impact
luna-2-impact.description: Hit the Moon: reaching another world, even by crashing into it.

pioneer-2-orbit.name: Lunar orbit
pioneer-2-orbit.description: Fire the probe's own motor to brake into orbit around the Moon.

lunar-orbiter-mapping.name: Lunar mapping
lunar-orbiter-mapping.description: Photograph the Moon from orbit to find safe landing sites.

surveyor-landing.name: Soft landing
surveyor-landing.description: Land gently on the Moon and photograph and probe the ground around the lander.

luna-15-sample-return.name: Sample return
luna-15-sample-return.description: Land, drill into the surface, and launch the sample back to Earth in a sealed capsule.

luna-3-flyby.name: Far side flyby
luna-3-flyby.description: Loop around the Moon and photograph the side the Earth never sees.

luna-17-landing.name: Landing with a rover
luna-17-landing.description: Land and drive the rover off its ramps to explore the surface by remote control.

pioneer-sun-orbit.name: Solar orbit
pioneer-sun-orbit.description: Leave the Earth behind and measure the solar wind from an orbit around the Sun.

mariner-10-flyby.name: Venus and Mercury flyby
mariner-10-flyby.description: Swing past Venus and use its gravity to reach Mercury.

mariner-5-flyby.name: Venus flyby
mariner-5-flyby.description: Fly close past Venus and measure its atmosphere.

pioneer-venus-orbit.name: Venus orbit
pioneer-venus-orbit.description: Brake into orbit around Venus and map it by radar.

venera-15-orbit.name: Venus orbit
venera-15-orbit.description: Brake into orbit around Venus and map its surface by radar.

pioneer-venus-multiprobe-entry.name: Atmospheric probes
pioneer-venus-multiprobe-entry.description: Release the probes ahead of arrival and let them fall through Venus's atmosphere at four different points.

venera-7-landing.name: Venus landing
venera-7-landing.description: Send the capsule down through Venus's atmosphere and keep it talking from the surface.

venera-flyby-and-lander.name: Flyby and lander
venera-flyby-and-lander.description: The carrier flies past Venus and relays the lander's signal while the lander goes down.
venera-flyby-and-lander.historyNote: Venera 13 landed on 1 March 1982 and sent back the first color pictures from the surface of Venus: flat, slabby rocks and soil under an orange sky. It was built to last 32 minutes at about 457 degrees Celsius and 89 times the Earth's air pressure. It kept working for 127, a record no other lander on Venus has beaten.

venera-orbiter-and-lander.name: Orbiter and lander
venera-orbiter-and-lander.description: The carrier brakes into orbit and relays the lander's signal from the surface.

mariner-6-flyby.name: Mars flyby
mariner-6-flyby.description: Fly past Mars and photograph its surface.

mariner-9-orbit.name: Mars orbit
mariner-9-orbit.description: Brake into orbit around Mars and map the planet.

viking-orbiter-and-lander.name: Orbiter and lander
viking-orbiter-and-lander.description: Survey Mars from orbit, then land and test the soil for signs of life.

mars-2-orbiter-lander-rover.name: Orbiter, lander and rover
mars-2-orbiter-lander-rover.description: Brake into orbit, send the lander down, and walk the small rover across the surface.

mars-m69-orbit.name: Mars orbit
mars-m69-orbit.description: Brake into orbit around Mars and photograph the planet.

pioneer-10-flyby.name: Jupiter flyby
pioneer-10-flyby.description: Cross the asteroid belt and fly past Jupiter.

pioneer-11-flyby.name: Jupiter and Saturn flyby
pioneer-11-flyby.description: Fly past Jupiter and use its gravity to reach Saturn.

x-15-flight-test.name: Flight test
x-15-flight-test.description: Drop from the carrier aircraft, light the engine and prove the plane flies, before pushing for speed and height.
x-15-flight-test.historyNote: Scott Crossfield flew the X-15 for the first time on 8 June 1959, released from under a B-52's wing to glide down to a dry lake bed with no rocket fuel aboard. Its first powered flight, on 17 September, used two smaller interim engines: the big engine built for it wasn't ready yet. Crossfield reached about Mach 2.1.

x-15-research-flight-1.name: Research flight: altitude
x-15-research-flight-1.description: Climb steeply to the edge of space, where the thrusters steer and the pilot sees the black sky.
x-15-research-flight-1.historyNote: The US Air Force gave astronaut wings for flights above 50 miles, about 80 km, and eight X-15 pilots earned them. The civilian pilots from NASA didn't get theirs until 2005. On 15 November 1967 Michael Adams went into a spin at about Mach 5 coming down from 81 km, and his X-15 broke up: the program's only fatal accident in 199 flights.

x-15-research-flight-2.name: Research flight: speed
x-15-research-flight-2.description: Hold a fast, level run at several times the speed of sound, where friction with the air heats the skin to hundreds of degrees.
x-15-research-flight-2.historyNote: For its speed record of Mach 6.7 in October 1967, the X-15A-2 was coated in a pink layer meant to char away and carried a dummy ramjet engine under its tail. Shock waves from the dummy heated the structure beside it beyond what the coating could take, burned holes in the skin, and tore the dummy away. The real ramjet never flew.

mig-e-154-drop-test.name: Drop test
mig-e-154-drop-test.description: Dropped from under the carrier's belly, light the engines and prove the plane flies, before pushing for height and speed.

gemini-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
gemini-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the Gemini capsule without a crew on a short up-and-down hop, to prove the launch, the heat shield and the recovery before anyone rides it.
gemini-uncrewed-suborbital.historyNote: Gemini 2's first launch attempt, on 9 December 1964, lasted one second: the engines lit and shut down again when a cracked valve cost hydraulic pressure and the rocket's malfunction detection switched to its backup. It flew on 19 January 1965, an 18-minute arc to test the heat shield, and was fished out of the Atlantic.

gemini-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
gemini-suborbital.description: A crewed hop into space and straight back down: the Gemini capsule's first flight with people aboard.

gemini-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
gemini-uncrewed-orbital.description: Put an empty Gemini capsule into orbit and bring it home, to prove it can keep a crew alive there.
gemini-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: Gemini 1, on 8 April 1964, was never meant to come home. The capsule stayed attached to its rocket's second stage, and engineers drilled four holes in its heat shield so it would be sure to burn up on reentry. Tracking stations followed it for four days until it came down over the South Atlantic.

gemini-orbital.name: Orbital flight
gemini-orbital.description: A crewed flight around the Earth in the Gemini capsule, and a safe return.
gemini-orbital.historyNote: Gemini 3, in March 1965, was the first American flight to change its own orbit. Gus Grissom named the capsule Molly Brown, after a musical about an unsinkable woman: his Mercury capsule had sunk. John Young smuggled a corned beef sandwich aboard. The crumbs could have fouled the electronics, and the crew were reprimanded.

gemini-spacewalk.name: Spacewalk (duration level I)
gemini-spacewalk.description: A longer flight in which one astronaut opens the hatch and goes outside on an umbilical.
gemini-spacewalk.historyNote: Ed White stepped out of Gemini 4 on 3 June 1965 with a small gas gun to push himself around. It ran dry after about three minutes, and he moved by tugging on his tether. Ordered back in as the spacecraft headed into darkness, he called it the saddest moment of his life. Then the hatch wouldn't latch, and the two of them fought it closed.

gemini-rendezvous.name: Rendezvous
gemini-rendezvous.description: Launch two Gemini capsules and steer one to within a few meters of the other.
gemini-rendezvous.historyNote: On 12 December 1965 Gemini 6A's engines lit and shut down after about a second and a half, with the rocket still on the pad. The rules said to eject. Wally Schirra judged that they hadn't lifted off and stayed put, which saved the spacecraft and the mission. Three days later they launched and caught Gemini 7.

gemini-docking.name: Docking
gemini-docking.description: Launch an Agena target, then a Gemini that finds it and docks.
gemini-docking.historyNote: Gemini 10, in July 1966, docked with its own Agena, used its engine to climb, and then went after a second target: the Agena left in orbit by Gemini 8 four months earlier. Michael Collins spacewalked across to it on a tether and retrieved a dust collector that had been waiting there since March, the first visit to another spacecraft in orbit.

gemini-spacewalk-and-rendezvous.name: Spacewalk and rendezvous (duration I)
gemini-spacewalk-and-rendezvous.description: A rendezvous between two capsules, with a spacewalk as well.
gemini-spacewalk-and-rendezvous.historyNote: In June 1966 Gemini 9A's crew caught up with their target and found its nose cover still hanging open in two halves: it had failed to come off. Tom Stafford said it looked like an angry alligator. Docking was impossible, so they flew rendezvous practice around it instead.

gemini-spacewalk-and-docking.name: Spacewalk and docking (duration level I)
gemini-spacewalk-and-docking.description: Dock with an Agena, then step outside to work on it.
gemini-spacewalk-and-docking.historyNote: Gemini 12, in November 1966, was the last chance to make spacewalks work before Apollo. Buzz Aldrin had trained underwater for hours, the Gemini and its Agena were fitted with many more handholds, rails and foot restraints, and he paced himself with rests. His spacewalks went so smoothly that the problems of the earlier flights were seen as solved.

gemini-rendezvous-duration-2.name: Rendezvous (duration level II)
gemini-rendezvous-duration-2.description: A longer flight with a rendezvous between two capsules.

gemini-docking-duration-2.name: Docking (duration level II)
gemini-docking-duration-2.description: A longer flight, docked to an Agena and using its engine.
gemini-docking-duration-2.historyNote: In September 1966 Gemini 11's crew docked with their Agena and fired its engine for 25 seconds, swinging up to about 1,370 km above the Earth. No crew orbiting the Earth went higher again until 2024.

gemini-spacewalk-and-rendezvous-duration.name: Spacewalk and rendezvous (duration II)
gemini-spacewalk-and-rendezvous-duration.description: A longer flight with a rendezvous and a spacewalk.

gemini-spacewalk-and-docking-duration-2.name: Spacewalk and docking (duration II)
gemini-spacewalk-and-docking-duration-2.description: A longer flight, docked to an Agena, with work outside.

gemini-orbital-duration-3.name: Orbital flight (duration level III)
gemini-orbital-duration-3.description: A long stay in a cramped cabin, to prove a crew can last as long as a trip to the Moon and back takes.
gemini-orbital-duration-3.historyNote: Frank Borman and Jim Lovell spent almost 14 days in Gemini 7 in December 1965, in a cabin little bigger than the front seat of a small car. They were the first crew allowed to take their suits off in flight, and after some back and forth the managers agreed both men could fly without them. They stuffed their rubbish behind their seats.

circumlunar-gemini-heat-shield-test.name: Heat shield test
circumlunar-gemini-heat-shield-test.description: An uncrewed capsule driven back into the atmosphere at close to lunar return speed.

circumlunar-gemini-transtage-test.name: Transtage test
circumlunar-gemini-transtage-test.description: A crew docks with a Transtage in Earth orbit and fires it, and the capsule tests its heat shield on the way home.

lunar-orbital-gemini-heat-shield-test.name: Heat shield test
lunar-orbital-gemini-heat-shield-test.description: An uncrewed capsule driven back into the atmosphere at close to lunar return speed.

lunar-orbital-gemini-propulsion-module-t.name: Propulsion module test
lunar-orbital-gemini-propulsion-module-t.description: A crew fires the lunar propulsion module in Earth orbit before trusting it at the Moon.

gemini-direct-ascent-uncrewed-test.name: Uncrewed test
gemini-direct-ascent-uncrewed-test.description: Fly the direct-ascent craft without a crew and fire its landing and ascent modules in Earth orbit.

gemini-direct-ascent-crewed-test.name: Crewed test
gemini-direct-ascent-crewed-test.description: A crew flies the direct-ascent craft in Earth orbit and puts its modules through their paces.

voskhod-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
voskhod-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the Voskhod capsule without a crew on a short up-and-down hop, to prove the launch, the heat shield and the recovery before anyone rides it.

voskhod-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
voskhod-suborbital.description: A crewed hop into space and straight back down: the Voskhod capsule's first flight with people aboard.

voskhod-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
voskhod-uncrewed-orbital.description: Put an empty Voskhod capsule into orbit and bring it home, to prove it can keep a crew alive there.
voskhod-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: Before three cosmonauts rode a Voskhod, an empty one was tested in secret. It was announced as Kosmos 47, launched on 6 October 1964, and spent a day in orbit while its systems were tested. It landed on 7 October, and Voskhod 1 went up five days later with its crew.

voskhod-orbital.name: Orbital flight
voskhod-orbital.description: A crewed flight around the Earth in the Voskhod capsule, and a safe return.
voskhod-orbital.historyNote: Voskhod 1's crew of three included the first doctor and the first engineer in space. Boris Yegorov watched his crewmates' health; Konstantin Feoktistov had helped design the spacecraft itself, the only Soviet spacecraft designer ever to fly in space. Korolev had insisted on putting him on the crew.

voskhod-orbital-duration-1.name: Orbital flight (duration level I)
voskhod-orbital-duration-1.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Voskhod, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

voskhod-orbital-duration-2.name: Orbital flight (duration level II)
voskhod-orbital-duration-2.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Voskhod, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.
voskhod-orbital-duration-2.historyNote: The longest Voskhod flight carried two dogs. Veterok and Ugolyok, picked from about a hundred strays, launched on 22 February 1966 as Kosmos 110 and orbited for 22 days, passing through the inner radiation belt. They came back dehydrated, thin and weak, and took weeks to recover. No crew stayed up as long until Soyuz 11 in 1971.

voskhod-orbital-duration-3.name: Orbital flight (duration level III)
voskhod-orbital-duration-3.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Voskhod, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

voskhod-orbital-duration-4.name: Orbital flight (duration level IV)
voskhod-orbital-duration-4.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Voskhod, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

voskhod-spacewalk.name: Spacewalk
voskhod-spacewalk.description: One cosmonaut crawls through the inflatable airlock and floats outside on a tether.
voskhod-spacewalk.historyNote: Voskhod 2's trip home went wrong. The automatic retrofire failed, and Pavel Belyayev fired it by hand for the first time in Soviet spaceflight. The capsule came down far off target in snowy forest in the Ural Mountains, and rescuers only reached the cosmonauts the next day. They were flown out by helicopter on 21 March 1965.

voskhod-joint-orbital.name: Joint flight
voskhod-joint-orbital.description: Two Voskhod craft launched in quick succession into nearly the same orbit, flying close enough to see each other.

soyuz-7k-l1-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
soyuz-7k-l1-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the Soyuz 7K-L1 without a crew on a short up-and-down hop, to prove the launch, the heat shield and the recovery before anyone rides it.

soyuz-7k-l1-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
soyuz-7k-l1-suborbital.description: A crewed hop into space and straight back down: the Soyuz 7K-L1's first flight with people aboard.

soyuz-7k-l1-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
soyuz-7k-l1-uncrewed-orbital.description: Put an empty Soyuz 7K-L1 into orbit and bring it home, to prove it can keep a crew alive there.
soyuz-7k-l1-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: One of the first attempts to send a 7K-L1 around the Moon, Kosmos 154 in April 1967, never left Earth orbit. A switch had been left in the wrong position during preparation, so the small rockets that settle the fuel before its Block D stage could restart were thrown away too early. The stage never fired again.

soyuz-7k-l1-orbital.name: Orbital flight
soyuz-7k-l1-orbital.description: A crewed flight around the Earth in the Soyuz 7K-L1, and a safe return.

soyuz-7k-l1-orbital-duration-1.name: Orbital flight (duration level I)
soyuz-7k-l1-orbital-duration-1.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz 7K-L1, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-l1-orbital-duration-2.name: Orbital flight (duration level II)
soyuz-7k-l1-orbital-duration-2.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz 7K-L1, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the Soyuz 7K-LOK without a crew on a short up-and-down hop, to prove the launch, the heat shield and the recovery before anyone rides it.

soyuz-7k-l3-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
soyuz-7k-l3-suborbital.description: A crewed hop into space and straight back down: the Soyuz 7K-LOK's first flight with people aboard.

soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-orbital.description: Put an empty Soyuz 7K-LOK into orbit and bring it home, to prove it can keep a crew alive there.

soyuz-7k-l3-orbital.name: Orbital flight
soyuz-7k-l3-orbital.description: A crewed flight around the Earth in the Soyuz 7K-LOK, and a safe return.

soyuz-7k-l3-orbital-duration-1.name: Orbital flight (duration level I)
soyuz-7k-l3-orbital-duration-1.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz 7K-LOK, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-l3-orbital-duration-2.name: Orbital flight (duration level II)
soyuz-7k-l3-orbital-duration-2.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz 7K-LOK, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-l3-orbital-duration-3.name: Orbital flight (duration level III)
soyuz-7k-l3-orbital-duration-3.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz 7K-LOK, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-l3-spacewalk.name: Spacewalk
soyuz-7k-l3-spacewalk.description: A cosmonaut leaves the craft in a spacesuit, as one would cross to the lander at the Moon.

soyuz-7k-l3-joint-orbital.name: Joint flight
soyuz-7k-l3-joint-orbital.description: Two Soyuz craft launched in quick succession into nearly the same orbit, flying close enough to see each other.

soyuz-7k-l3-automatic-rendezvous.name: Automatic rendezvous
soyuz-7k-l3-automatic-rendezvous.description: Two uncrewed craft find each other in orbit under automatic control.

soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-lander-test.name: Uncrewed LK test
soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-lander-test.description: Put the LK lander into Earth orbit without a crew and fire its engine as it would land and lift off at the Moon.

soyuz-7k-l3-lander-test.name: LK test
soyuz-7k-l3-lander-test.description: A cosmonaut flies the LK in Earth orbit and tests the landing and ascent burns.

lk-700-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
lk-700-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the LK-700 without a crew on a short up-and-down hop, to prove the launch, the heat shield and the recovery before anyone rides it.

lk-700-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
lk-700-suborbital.description: A crewed hop into space and straight back down: the LK-700's first flight with people aboard.

lk-700-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
lk-700-uncrewed-orbital.description: Put an empty LK-700 into orbit and bring it home, to prove it can keep a crew alive there.

lk-700-orbital.name: Orbital flight
lk-700-orbital.description: A crewed flight around the Earth in the LK-700, and a safe return.

lk-700-orbital-duration-1.name: Orbital flight (duration level I)
lk-700-orbital-duration-1.description: A longer stay in orbit in the LK-700, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

lk-700-orbital-duration-2.description: A longer stay in orbit in the LK-700, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

lk-700-orbital-duration-6.description: A longer stay in orbit in the LK-700, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

lk-700-spacewalk.name: Spacewalk
lk-700-spacewalk.description: A crew member leaves the LK-700 in a pressure suit, on a tether, and works outside.

gemini-eor-lander-test.name: Lander test in low orbit
gemini-eor-lander-test.description: Deploy the light lander in low Earth orbit and test its engine and ascent.

gemini-eor-lander-and-heat-shield-test.name: Lander and heat shield test
gemini-eor-lander-and-heat-shield-test.description: Test the lander in a higher orbit, then dive back at high speed to test the heat shield.

circumlunar-gemini-transtage-flyby.name: Uncrewed lunar flyby
circumlunar-gemini-transtage-flyby.description: Push an empty capsule around the Moon with the Transtage and bring it home.

circumlunar-gemini-flyby.name: Lunar flyby (duration level II)
circumlunar-gemini-flyby.description: A crew docks with the Transtage, swings around the Moon and comes home.

lunar-orbital-gemini-uncrewed-flyby.name: Uncrewed lunar flyby
lunar-orbital-gemini-uncrewed-flyby.description: Send the empty craft around the Moon and home again.

lunar-orbital-gemini-flyby.name: Lunar flyby (duration level II)
lunar-orbital-gemini-flyby.description: A crew flies around the Moon and home.

lunar-orbital-gemini-lunar-orbit.name: Lunar orbit (duration level II)
lunar-orbital-gemini-lunar-orbit.description: A crew brakes into orbit around the Moon, circles it and returns.

gemini-direct-ascent-uncrewed-flyby.name: Uncrewed lunar flyby
gemini-direct-ascent-uncrewed-flyby.description: Send the empty craft around the Moon and home again.

gemini-direct-ascent-flyby.name: Lunar flyby (duration level II)
gemini-direct-ascent-flyby.description: A crew flies around the Moon and home.

gemini-direct-ascent-uncrewed-lunar-orbi.name: Uncrewed lunar orbit
gemini-direct-ascent-uncrewed-lunar-orbi.description: Brake an empty craft into lunar orbit and fire it home again.

gemini-direct-ascent-lunar-orbit.name: Lunar orbit (duration level II)
gemini-direct-ascent-lunar-orbit.description: A crew brakes into lunar orbit, circles the Moon and returns.

gemini-direct-ascent-landing.name: Lunar landing
gemini-direct-ascent-landing.description: The whole craft lands on the Moon, the crew goes out, and it lifts off for home.

apollo-uncrewed-flyby.name: Uncrewed lunar flyby
apollo-uncrewed-flyby.description: Send an empty Apollo around the Moon and bring it home at lunar return speed.

apollo-flyby.name: Lunar flyby (duration level II)
apollo-flyby.description: A crew loops around the Moon and returns.
apollo-flyby.historyNote: After an oxygen tank exploded in April 1970, Apollo 13 swung around the Moon on a free-return path instead of landing, and fired the lunar module's engine to get back onto it. The crew reached about 400,000 km from home, a record for human travel that stood until Artemis II in April 2026.

apollo-uncrewed-lunar-orbit.name: Uncrewed lunar orbit
apollo-uncrewed-lunar-orbit.description: Brake an empty Apollo into lunar orbit and fire it home again.

apollo-lunar-orbit.name: Lunar orbit (duration level II)
apollo-lunar-orbit.description: A crew brakes into orbit around the Moon, circles it, and comes home.
apollo-lunar-orbit.historyNote: On 24 December 1968, on Apollo 8's fourth orbit of the Moon, the spacecraft turned and the Earth came up over the lunar horizon. Nobody had planned for it. Bill Anders took a black-and-white frame, called for a color magazine, and caught the Earth again in another window within about a minute. The picture became known as Earthrise.

apollo-lander-test.name: Lander test in lunar orbit
apollo-lander-test.description: A full rehearsal: the lunar module descends close to the surface, climbs back and docks, but doesn't land.
apollo-lander-test.historyNote: In May 1969 Apollo 10's lunar module Snoopy dropped to about 14 km above the Moon, scouting Apollo 11's landing approach. When the crew separated the ascent stage, it lurched and tumbled because a switch had been left in the wrong position, and Tom Stafford and Gene Cernan swore on the open radio while they regained control.

apollo-landing.name: Lunar landing
apollo-landing.description: Two astronauts land, walk on the Moon and collect rocks, then rejoin the command module in orbit.
apollo-landing.historyNote: Apollo 12 was struck by lightning twice in its first minute, on 14 November 1969, and the spacecraft's instruments went haywire. Flight controller John Aaron recognized the pattern from a test and called for an obscure switch, SCE to AUX. Only Alan Bean knew where it was. He flipped it, the readings came back, and the mission went on to the Moon.

apollo-landing-with-rover.name: Lunar landing with rover
apollo-landing-with-rover.description: A longer stay on the Moon with the rover, driving far from the lander to explore.
apollo-landing-with-rover.historyNote: Apollo 15, in July 1971, was the first to take a lunar rover. David Scott and James Irwin drove about 28 km on three trips across the Hadley-Apennine region, to the edge of the deep canyon of Hadley Rille and up the slopes of the mountains. They brought back an ancient piece of the Moon's early crust, nicknamed the Genesis Rock.

gemini-eor-flyby.name: Lunar flyby (duration level II)
gemini-eor-flyby.description: Assemble the craft in Earth orbit and send a crew around the Moon.

gemini-eor-lunar-orbit.name: Lunar orbit (duration level II)
gemini-eor-lunar-orbit.description: Assemble the craft in Earth orbit and brake into orbit around the Moon.

gemini-eor-lander-test-lunar-orbit.name: Lander test in lunar orbit
gemini-eor-lander-test-lunar-orbit.description: Fly the light lander down toward the Moon and back up to the waiting capsule, without landing.

gemini-eor-landing.name: Lunar landing
gemini-eor-landing.description: One astronaut rides the open lander down to the Moon and back up to the capsule.

soyuz-7k-l1-uncrewed-flyby.name: Uncrewed lunar flyby
soyuz-7k-l1-uncrewed-flyby.description: Send an empty craft around the Moon and bring it home.
soyuz-7k-l1-uncrewed-flyby.historyNote: Zond 7, in August 1969, was the 7K-L1 flight that went right. It photographed the Earth and the Moon in color, came home by skipping off the upper atmosphere to shed speed, and landed in the planned area in Kazakhstan. With a crew aboard it would have been the first safe Soviet trip around the Moon, but by then Apollo 11 had landed.

soyuz-7k-l1-flyby.name: Lunar flyby (duration level II)
soyuz-7k-l1-flyby.description: Two cosmonauts loop around the Moon and come straight back.

soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-flyby.name: Uncrewed lunar flyby
soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-flyby.description: Send an empty craft around the Moon and home.

soyuz-7k-l3-flyby.name: Lunar flyby (duration level II)
soyuz-7k-l3-flyby.description: A crew loops around the Moon and returns.

soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-lunar-orbit.name: Uncrewed lunar orbit
soyuz-7k-l3-uncrewed-lunar-orbit.description: Brake an empty craft into lunar orbit and fire it home again.

soyuz-7k-l3-lunar-orbit.name: Lunar orbit (duration level II)
soyuz-7k-l3-lunar-orbit.description: A crew brakes into lunar orbit and returns.

soyuz-7k-l3-lander-test-lunar-orbit.name: Lander test in lunar orbit
soyuz-7k-l3-lander-test-lunar-orbit.description: A cosmonaut crosses to the LK, flies it in lunar orbit and returns.

soyuz-7k-l3-landing.name: Lunar landing
soyuz-7k-l3-landing.description: One cosmonaut spacewalks to the LK, lands alone, and flies back up to the waiting Soyuz.

lk-700-uncrewed-flyby.name: Uncrewed lunar flyby
lk-700-uncrewed-flyby.description: Send an empty craft around the Moon and home.

lk-700-flyby.name: Lunar flyby (duration level II)
lk-700-flyby.description: A crew loops around the Moon and returns.

lk-700-uncrewed-lunar-orbit.description: Brake an empty craft into lunar orbit and fire it home again.

lk-700-lunar-orbit.description: A crew brakes into lunar orbit and returns.

lk-700-landing.name: Direct-ascent landing
lk-700-landing.description: The whole craft and crew land on the Moon and lift off again for home.

apollo-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
apollo-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the Apollo command module without a crew on a short up-and-down hop, to prove the launch, the heat shield and the recovery before anyone rides it.
apollo-uncrewed-suborbital.historyNote: The first flight of an Apollo command and service module, AS-201 on 26 February 1966, was a 37-minute hop on the first Saturn IB. The heat shield held up, but helium bubbles reached the main engine and its pressure dropped 30 percent, and an electrical fault set the capsule rolling through reentry.

apollo-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
apollo-suborbital.description: A crewed hop into space and straight back down: the Apollo command module's first flight with people aboard.

apollo-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
apollo-uncrewed-orbital.description: Put an empty Apollo spacecraft into orbit and bring it home, to prove it can keep a crew alive there.
apollo-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: Apollo 4, on 9 November 1967, was the first flight of the Saturn V, and every stage flew live on the first try. Five kilometers away, the roof of CBS's viewing booth shed tiles, and Walter Cronkite told viewers on air that the building was shaking and they were holding the window with their hands. The capsule came home at Moon-return speed to test its heat shield.

apollo-orbital.name: Orbital flight
apollo-orbital.description: A crewed flight around the Earth in the Apollo spacecraft, and a safe return.
apollo-orbital.historyNote: Apollo 7, in October 1968, was the first crewed Apollo, eleven days in Earth orbit, and the first American flight to send live television. All three crew caught heavy colds. Wally Schirra refused to start the first TV broadcast before their tests were done, and before reentry the crew refused to wear their helmets so they could blow their noses to clear their ears.

apollo-uncrewed-lunar-module-test.name: Uncrewed lunar module test
apollo-uncrewed-lunar-module-test.description: Fly the lunar module alone in Earth orbit and fire both its stages.
apollo-uncrewed-lunar-module-test.historyNote: The first lunar module flew in January 1968 on Apollo 5, without a crew. Its computer cut the first descent-engine burn short after about four seconds of a planned 39. Gene Kranz's team in Houston switched to a backup plan and fired the engines by command, including the ascent engine while still attached to the descent stage, as it would in an abort.

apollo-lunar-module-test-low-orbit.name: Lunar module test in low orbit
apollo-lunar-module-test-low-orbit.description: The crew separates the lunar module, flies it apart, and docks again, with a spacewalk.
apollo-lunar-module-test-low-orbit.historyNote: On Apollo 9 Russell Schweickart was space sick on the first day, so his planned spacewalk to the command module was cut back. Instead he stood on the lunar module's front porch for about 40 minutes, the first American spacewalk on a backpack of his own instead of a hose to the spacecraft: the backpack the Moon walkers would wear.

apollo-lunar-module-test-high-orbit.name: Lunar module test in high orbit
apollo-lunar-module-test-high-orbit.description: The same rehearsal in a high orbit, ending in a fast reentry to test the heat shield.
apollo-lunar-module-test-high-orbit.historyNote: Apollo 6, in April 1968, shook. Its first stage bounced along its length, two of the five engines of the second stage shut down early, and the third stage would not restart. Fuel lines for the engines' igniters had leaked and failed, and a cross-wired cable had shut down the healthy engine beside the bad one. Engineers fixed it all, and the next Saturn V carried a crew.

apollo-orbital-duration-1.name: Orbital flight (duration level I)
apollo-orbital-duration-1.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Apollo, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

apollo-orbital-duration-2.name: Orbital flight (duration level II)
apollo-orbital-duration-2.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Apollo, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

apollo-orbital-duration-3.name: Orbital flight (duration level III)
apollo-orbital-duration-3.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Apollo, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

apollo-orbital-duration-4.name: Orbital flight (duration level IV)
apollo-orbital-duration-4.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Apollo, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.
apollo-orbital-duration-4.historyNote: The longest Apollo flight never left Earth orbit. Skylab's last crew rode an Apollo command and service module up to the station in November 1973, left it docked for 83 days, and came home in it in February 1974 after 84 days. For more than 20 years no American flew longer.

apollo-spacewalk-duration-1.name: Spacewalk (duration level I)
apollo-spacewalk-duration-1.description: A longer orbital flight with work outside the spacecraft.

apollo-spacewalk-duration-2.name: Spacewalk (duration level II)
apollo-spacewalk-duration-2.description: A longer orbital flight with work outside the spacecraft.

apollo-spacewalk-duration-3.name: Spacewalk (duration level III)
apollo-spacewalk-duration-3.description: A long orbital flight with work outside the spacecraft.

apollo-spacewalk-duration-4.name: Spacewalk (duration level IV)
apollo-spacewalk-duration-4.description: A very long orbital flight with work outside the spacecraft.

apollo-rendezvous.name: Rendezvous
apollo-rendezvous.description: Two crewed Apollos launched to meet in orbit.

apollo-docking.name: Docking
apollo-docking.description: An Apollo docks with a target launched ahead of it.
apollo-docking.historyNote: In July 1975 an Apollo docked with a Soyuz that had launched seven and a half hours ahead of it. The two craft breathed different air: Apollo pure oxygen at about a third of an atmosphere, Soyuz a nitrogen-oxygen mix near sea-level pressure. A docking module between them worked as an airlock, and the Soyuz crew lowered their cabin pressure to make the crossing easier.

soyuz-7k-ok-uncrewed-suborbital.name: Uncrewed suborbital test
soyuz-7k-ok-uncrewed-suborbital.description: Fly the Soyuz without a crew on a short up-and-down hop, to prove the launch, the heat shield and the recovery before anyone rides it.

soyuz-7k-ok-suborbital.name: Suborbital flight
soyuz-7k-ok-suborbital.description: A crewed hop into space and straight back down: the Soyuz's first flight with people aboard.

soyuz-7k-ok-uncrewed-orbital.name: Uncrewed orbital test
soyuz-7k-ok-uncrewed-orbital.description: Put an empty Soyuz into orbit and bring it home, to prove it can keep a crew alive there.
soyuz-7k-ok-uncrewed-orbital.historyNote: The first empty Soyuz, Kosmos 133 in November 1966, ran out of attitude fuel and came down on a path toward China, so it was blown up. The next one exploded on the pad when its escape rocket fired by mistake. The third, Kosmos 140 in February 1967, burned a hole in its heat shield and crashed through the ice of the Aral Sea.

soyuz-7k-ok-orbital.name: Orbital flight
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital.description: A crewed flight around the Earth in the Soyuz, and a safe return.
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital.historyNote: Soyuz 1 launched on 23 April 1967 with Vladimir Komarov alone aboard. One of its two solar panels never opened, power ran short, and its sensors misbehaved, so the mission was cut short. On reentry the main parachute failed to come out and the reserve tangled with it. Komarov was killed on impact, the first person to die on a spaceflight.

soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-1.name: Orbital flight (duration level I)
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-1.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-2.name: Orbital flight (duration level II)
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-2.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-3.name: Orbital flight (duration level III)
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-3.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-4.name: Orbital flight (duration level IV)
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-4.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-4.historyNote: In June 1970 Andriyan Nikolayev and Vitaly Sevastyanov stayed up in Soyuz 9 for almost 18 days, breaking the record Gemini 7 had held since 1965. To save fuel the craft was spun slowly, which left them dizzy and sick. After landing they had to be helped out and could hardly walk for days: the first clear warning of what long flights do to the body.

soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-5.name: Orbital flight (duration level V)
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-5.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-6.name: Orbital flight (duration level VI)
soyuz-7k-ok-orbital-duration-6.description: A longer stay in orbit in the Soyuz, to learn how people and machines hold up over time.

soyuz-7k-ok-spacewalk.name: Spacewalk
soyuz-7k-ok-spacewalk.description: A crew member leaves the Soyuz in a pressure suit, on a tether, and works outside.

soyuz-7k-ok-joint-orbital.name: Joint flight
soyuz-7k-ok-joint-orbital.description: Two Soyuz craft launched in quick succession into nearly the same orbit, flying close enough to see each other.
soyuz-7k-ok-joint-orbital.historyNote: In October 1969 three Soyuz craft flew together with seven cosmonauts aboard. Soyuz 7 and 8 were meant to dock but couldn't: their Igla systems failed. On Soyuz 6, Valeri Kubasov tried welding in space for the first time, with three methods, and nearly burned through the wall of the cabin.

soyuz-7k-ok-automatic-rendezvous.name: Automatic rendezvous
soyuz-7k-ok-automatic-rendezvous.description: Two craft find each other in orbit with the Igla system steering.

soyuz-7k-ok-uncrewed-docking.name: Uncrewed docking
soyuz-7k-ok-uncrewed-docking.description: Two empty Soyuz craft find each other and dock automatically.

soyuz-7k-ok-crewed-docking.name: Crewed docking
soyuz-7k-ok-crewed-docking.description: A crewed Soyuz docks with a second craft under the Igla system's guidance.
soyuz-7k-ok-crewed-docking.historyNote: In October 1968 Georgy Beregovoy in Soyuz 3 approached the uncrewed Soyuz 2 and took over by hand at about 180 meters. In the dark he failed to notice that the target was turned upside down relative to his craft, and his attempts to dock used up most of his fuel. The Soviet Union announced a success; the planned docking was only admitted in the 1980s.

soyuz-7k-ok-crew-transfer.name: Docking and crew transfer
soyuz-7k-ok-crew-transfer.description: Two crewed Soyuz craft dock, and cosmonauts spacewalk from one to the other.

mig-e-154-research-flight-1.name: Research flight: altitude
mig-e-154-research-flight-1.description: Climb steeply out of the air to the edge of space, steering with thrusters where the wings have nothing to grip.

mig-e-154-research-flight-2.name: Research flight: speed
mig-e-154-research-flight-2.description: A fast, level run at several times the speed of sound, the skin heating as the air rushes past.

launch-preparations.name: Launch preparations
launch-preparations.description: Fueling, checks and loading the payload. Liquid oxygen boils away at minus 183 degrees Celsius, so it goes in last and is topped up until the final minutes.

countdown.name: Countdown
countdown.description: The final sequence before ignition. Any reading outside its limits stops the clock, and a long hold can push the launch to another day.

launch.name: Launch
launch.description: Ignition and liftoff. The first seconds are the most dangerous: the rocket is full of propellant and barely moving, and a failing engine can bring it down on the pad.

ascent.name: Ascent
ascent.description: Climbing through the thick lower air, past the point of greatest aerodynamic stress, and on to staging. Steering errors here decide whether the payload reaches the planned orbit.

deployment.name: Deployment
deployment.description: The payload separates from the last stage. Springs or small rockets push the two apart so they don't collide.

earth-orbit.name: Earth orbit
earth-orbit.description: Circling the Earth about every hour and a half, sending what it measures to ground stations as it passes over them.

earth-orbital.name: Earth orbit
earth-orbital.description: Circling the Earth about every hour and a half, sending what it measures to ground stations as it passes over them.

orbital-flight.name: Orbital flight
orbital-flight.description: Falling around the Earth about once every ninety minutes. Ground stations can only talk to the craft for a few minutes as it passes overhead.

suborbital-flight.name: Suborbital flight
suborbital-flight.description: Too slow to stay in orbit, the craft coasts on a ballistic arc above the atmosphere: a few minutes of weightlessness before it falls back.

advanced-experiments-earth-orbit.name: Extended experiments in orbit
advanced-experiments-earth-orbit.description: More time in orbit for longer measurements, as long as the batteries and the instruments hold out.

biometric-data-transmission.name: Biometric data transmission
biometric-data-transmission.description: Sensors on the passenger send back heartbeat, breathing and movement: the first data on how a living body copes with launch and weightlessness.

reentry-preparations.name: Reentry preparations
reentry-preparations.description: Turning the craft so its retrorockets point forward along its path, and checking the alignment. Firing at the wrong angle can bring it down far off target.

retrofire.name: Retrofire
retrofire.description: The retrorockets fire against the direction of travel. Losing only a small fraction of orbital speed is enough to lower the orbit into the atmosphere.

retrofire-jettison.name: Retropack jettison
retrofire-jettison.description: The spent retrorocket pack is cast off, so that it doesn't burn up against the heat shield.

modules-separation.name: Modules separation
modules-separation.description: The capsule separates from its equipment module, which burns up on its own. If the two stay joined, they tumble together in the thickening air.

reentry.name: Reentry
reentry.description: Hitting the air at around 28,000 km/h, the craft is slowed by the air piling up ahead of it. That air turns to glowing plasma, which blocks the radio for several minutes.

descent-and-landing.name: Descent and landing
descent-and-landing.description: Parachutes open a few kilometers up. On a crewed flight the pilot ejects and lands under a separate parachute, because the capsule hits the ground too hard.

descent-and-splashdown.name: Descent and splashdown
descent-and-splashdown.description: Parachutes slow the capsule for a landing at sea, where ships and helicopters wait to recover it before it takes on water.

duration-level-i.name: A day in orbit
duration-level-i.description: Staying up for a day or more: eating, sleeping and working in weightlessness, while doctors on the ground watch the pilot's health.

duration-level-ii.name: Several days in orbit
duration-level-ii.description: Days in orbit, near the limit of the capsule's oxygen, power and food.

joint-orbital-flight.name: Flying together
joint-orbital-flight.description: Both craft in orbit close to each other, talking by radio. With no engines to change their orbits, they slowly drift apart.

pre-launch.name: Preflight
pre-launch.description: The plane is fueled and checked, the pilot strapped in, and the carrier aircraft readied for takeoff.

takeoff.name: Carrier takeoff
takeoff.description: The carrier aircraft takes off with the rocket plane hanging beneath it and climbs to the release height.

launch-from-drop-plane.name: Drop and ignition
launch-from-drop-plane.description: Released from the carrier, the plane falls clear before the pilot lights the rocket engine.

powered-ascent.name: Powered climb
powered-ascent.description: The engine burns for a minute or two, pushing the plane steeply up or fast along.

peak-altitude.name: Peak altitude
peak-altitude.description: At the top of the arc the air is too thin for the wings; small thrusters hold the plane's attitude.

high-speed-leg.name: High-speed run
high-speed-leg.description: A fast run where friction with the air heats the skin and every control input matters.

de-orbit-burn.name: Deorbit burn
de-orbit-burn.description: An engine burn against the direction of flight drops the orbit into the atmosphere.

descent.name: Descent
descent.description: Down through the atmosphere, slowing as the air thickens, to parachutes or a glide.

landing.name: Landing
landing.description: Touchdown, whether on a runway, on land under parachutes or on another world.

landing-and-recovery.name: Landing and recovery
landing-and-recovery.description: Touchdown, and recovery teams reach the craft and its crew.

splashdown.name: Splashdown
splashdown.description: The capsule hits the sea under its parachutes.

splashdown-and-recovery.name: Splashdown and recovery
splashdown-and-recovery.description: The capsule lands in the sea and ships and helicopters pick up the crew.

recovery.name: Recovery
recovery.description: Ships, aircraft or ground teams reach the craft and bring it and its crew home.

insertion.name: Orbit insertion
insertion.description: The last burn of the climb, which leaves the craft in its planned orbit.

orbit-insertion.name: Orbit insertion
orbit-insertion.description: A burn that puts the craft into the orbit the mission needs.

parking-orbit.name: Parking orbit
parking-orbit.description: A low orbit to check the spacecraft over before committing to the next burn.

duration.name: Long stay in orbit
duration.description: Days in orbit while the crew and the systems are watched for wear.

duration-l5.name: Duration level V
duration-l5.description: Weeks in orbit while the crew and the systems are watched for wear.

duration-l6.name: Duration level VI
duration-l6.description: The longest stay yet, testing how long people can live and work in space.

duration-level-iii.name: Duration level III
duration-level-iii.description: A long stay in orbit while the crew and the systems are watched for wear.

duration-level-iv.name: Duration level IV
duration-level-iv.description: A very long stay in orbit while the crew and the systems are watched for wear.

joint-earth-orbital.name: Joint orbit
joint-earth-orbital.description: Two craft in nearly the same orbit, close enough to meet.

meo.name: High orbit
meo.description: Flying in a high orbit, far out where reentry speeds approach those of a lunar return.

injection-to-elliptical-meo.name: Burn to high orbit
injection-to-elliptical-meo.description: A burn that stretches the orbit far out from the Earth.

btm-earth-orbit.name: Burn to high orbit
btm-earth-orbit.description: An engine burn that raises the orbit far above the usual height.

co-apoa.name: Coast to high point
co-apoa.description: Coasting up to the highest point of a stretched orbit.

co-enin.name: Coast to reentry
co-enin.description: Coasting back toward the atmosphere, aimed for the narrow entry corridor.

ree-cor-adj-apoa.name: Entry corridor trim
ree-cor-adj-apoa.description: A small burn at the orbit's high point to aim the return into the narrow band between skipping off the air and burning up.

engine-test.name: Engine test
engine-test.description: The main engine is fired in space and checked against what the ground expects.

scientific-experiments.name: Spacewalk and experiments
scientific-experiments.description: Work outside the craft, setting up and recovering experiments.

target-approach.name: Target approach
target-approach.description: Closing on the target with small burns, the last stretch flown by eye or by radar.

rendezvous-target-approach.name: Closing in
rendezvous-target-approach.description: Burns that bring one craft up to the other, from many kilometers to a few meters.

rendezvous.name: Rendezvous
rendezvous.description: Two craft flying in formation, close enough to touch.

docking.name: Docking
docking.description: Easing together until the latches catch and the two craft are one.

approach-and-docking.name: Approach and docking
approach-and-docking.description: Closing on the waiting stage and docking with it.

rendezvous-and-docking.name: Rendezvous and docking
rendezvous-and-docking.description: The ascending craft catches up with the one waiting in orbit and docks.

at-docking.name: Automatic docking
at-docking.description: The craft dock under the control of their own radar and computers.

lll-docking.name: Lander docking
lll-docking.description: The lander docks with the capsule waiting in orbit.

undocking.name: Undocking
undocking.description: The latches open and the craft drift apart.

crew-transfer.name: Crew transfer
crew-transfer.description: Crew members cross from one craft to the other.

egress.name: Egress
egress.description: The hatch opens and an astronaut climbs out.

eva.name: Spacewalk
eva.description: Work outside the spacecraft in a pressure suit.

eva-i.name: First moonwalk
eva-i.description: The first walk on the surface: planting the flag and setting up experiments.

eva-ii.name: Second moonwalk
eva-ii.description: Another walk on the surface, ranging farther from the lander and collecting rocks to bring home.

eva-iii.name: Third moonwalk
eva-iii.description: A last walk on the surface, the rock boxes filled and carried up into the lander.

rover-trip-i.name: First rover drive
rover-trip-i.description: The crew unfold the rover from the lander's side and drive it out to the first sites.

rover-trip-ii.name: Second rover drive
rover-trip-ii.description: A longer drive, kilometres from the lander, stopping to sample and photograph.

eva-in-meo.name: Spacewalk in high orbit
eva-in-meo.description: Work outside the spacecraft far out from the Earth.

eva-7k-lok.name: Spacewalk to the lander
eva-7k-lok.description: A crew member crosses outside to the lander in a spacesuit.

eva-7k-ok.name: Spacewalk
eva-7k-ok.description: Work outside the spacecraft in a pressure suit.

eva-gemini-langley.name: Spacewalk to the lander
eva-gemini-langley.description: The astronaut leaves the capsule and climbs onto the open lander.

soyuz-7k-ok-deployment.name: Soyuz separation
soyuz-7k-ok-deployment.description: The Soyuz separates from the rocket and unfolds its solar panels and antennas.

soyuz-7k-l3-lok-deployment.name: Soyuz separation
soyuz-7k-l3-lok-deployment.description: The lunar Soyuz separates from the rocket and unfolds its panels and antennas.

lk-700-deployment.name: LK-700 separation
lk-700-deployment.description: The LK-700 separates from the rocket and is checked out in orbit.

lem-tests-earth-orbit.name: Lunar module checkout
lem-tests-earth-orbit.description: The crew powers up the lunar module and checks every system in Earth orbit.

lem-descent-stage-test.name: Descent engine firing
lem-descent-stage-test.description: The lunar module's descent engine fires in orbit, throttled as it would be for a landing.

fire-in-the-hole.name: Fire in the hole
fire-in-the-hole.description: The ascent engine lights while the two stages are still joined, as in an abort during a landing, and drives the ascent stage off the descent stage.

lem-ascent-stage-test.name: Ascent stage test
lem-ascent-stage-test.description: The ascent stage fires and separates from the descent stage, as it would to leave the Moon.

lem-jettison.name: Lunar module jettison
lem-jettison.description: The empty ascent stage is cut loose once the crew is back.

lk-test.name: LK engine test
lk-test.description: The LK's engine is fired as for the last part of a landing.

lk-lander-deployment.name: LK separation
lk-lander-deployment.description: The LK separates from the rocket and is checked out in orbit.

blok-d-separation.name: Blok D separation
blok-d-separation.description: The Blok D upper stage, its burns done, separates from the spacecraft.

lpu-jes-eng-res.name: Landing gear jettison and restart
lpu-jes-eng-res.description: The LK drops its landing gear and restarts its engine, as it would to lift off from the Moon.

langley-test-lld.name: Lander deployment
langley-test-lld.description: The light lander is released and checked out.

langley-test-lllet.name: Lander engine test
langley-test-lllet.description: The lander's engine is fired as for a landing.

langley-test-erat.name: Restart and ascent test
langley-test-erat.description: The lander restarts its engine and climbs as it would from the Moon.

lun-prop-mod-test.name: Propulsion module burn
lun-prop-mod-test.description: The lunar propulsion module fires as it would to brake at the Moon.

dir-asc-lan-mod-test.name: Landing module burn
dir-asc-lan-mod-test.description: The landing module fires as it would for the descent to the Moon.

dir-asc-mod-test-orb-apoa.name: Ascent module burn
dir-asc-mod-test-orb-apoa.description: The ascent module fires at the orbit's high point, as it would to leave the Moon.

ignition-and-separation.name: Transtage burn
ignition-and-separation.description: The Transtage fires to push the capsule toward the Moon, then separates.

high-orbit-injection.name: High-orbit injection
high-orbit-injection.description: A burn that stretches the orbit into a long ellipse, out far from the Earth and back, so the capsule falls into the air at nearly the speed of a return from the Moon.

tli.name: Trans-lunar injection
tli.description: The burn that breaks out of Earth orbit onto a path to the Moon.

trans-lunar-coast.name: Coast to the Moon
trans-lunar-coast.description: Three days or so of coasting, with small course corrections.

earth-moon-coast.name: Coast to the Moon
earth-moon-coast.description: Coasting from the Earth to the Moon, with small course corrections.

lunar-approach.name: Lunar approach
lunar-approach.description: Falling toward the Moon, aimed to pass at just the right height.

lunar-flyby.name: Lunar flyby
lunar-flyby.description: Swinging around the Moon, its gravity bending the path back toward the Earth.

loi.name: Lunar orbit insertion
loi.description: A braking burn behind the Moon that lets its gravity capture the craft.

lunar-orbit.name: Lunar orbit
lunar-orbit.description: Circling the Moon about every two hours, out of contact on every pass behind it.

transposition.name: Transposition and docking
transposition.description: The spacecraft turns around, docks with the lander nose to nose, and pulls it free of the rocket.

extraction.name: Lander extraction
extraction.description: The docked spacecraft pulls the lander free of the rocket stage.

lander-release.name: Lander release
lander-release.description: The lander separates from its carrier.

powered-descent.name: Powered descent
powered-descent.description: The descent engine brakes the lander out of orbit and down to touchdown.

lk-deployment.name: LK separation
lk-deployment.description: The LK undocks from the orbiting Soyuz.

lk-descent.name: LK descent
lk-descent.description: The LK brakes out of lunar orbit and lands.

lunar-surface-activities.name: On the surface
lunar-surface-activities.description: Hours on the Moon: exploring, collecting rocks, setting up instruments.

lunar-surface-operations-robotic.name: Surface operations
lunar-surface-operations-robotic.description: Remote-controlled work on the surface: drilling, driving, photographing.

lunar-liftoff.name: Lunar liftoff
lunar-liftoff.description: The engine fires and the craft lifts off from the Moon.

lunar-ascent.name: Lunar ascent
lunar-ascent.description: Climbing from the surface back into lunar orbit.

ascent-from-lunar-surface.name: Liftoff from the Moon
ascent-from-lunar-surface.description: The return stage lifts off with its sample.

tei.name: Trans-Earth injection
tei.description: The burn behind the Moon that sends the craft home.

trans-earth-coast.name: Coast to the Earth
trans-earth-coast.description: Coasting home from the Moon, with small course corrections.

moon-earth-coast.name: Coast to the Earth
moon-earth-coast.description: Coasting home from the Moon, with small course corrections.

earth-approach.name: Earth approach
earth-approach.description: Aiming for the narrow entry corridor at about eleven kilometers a second.

earth-approach-and-reentry.name: Approach and reentry
earth-approach-and-reentry.description: Arrival from the Moon and a fiery reentry at lunar return speed.

lunar-impact.name: Impact
lunar-impact.description: The probe strikes the Moon, sending pictures or data until the end.

tpi.name: Trans-planetary injection
tpi.description: The burn that sends the probe out of the Earth's grip onto a path to another planet.

earth-departure.name: Earth departure
earth-departure.description: Leaving the Earth behind on the path to another planet.

earth-venus-transit.name: Cruise to Venus
earth-venus-transit.description: Months of cruise to Venus, with course corrections on the way.

earth-venus-approach.name: Venus approach
earth-venus-approach.description: Closing on Venus at the end of the cruise.

venus-approach.name: Venus approach
venus-approach.description: Closing on Venus, aimed for the planned flyby, orbit or entry.

venus-flyby.name: Venus flyby
venus-flyby.description: Passing close by Venus and taking measurements.

venus-orbit.name: Venus orbit
venus-orbit.description: Circling Venus and mapping or measuring it.

venus-mercury-transit.name: Cruise to Mercury
venus-mercury-transit.description: Bent by Venus's gravity, the probe falls inward toward Mercury.

mercury-flyby.name: Mercury flyby
mercury-flyby.description: Passing close by Mercury and photographing it.

big-probe-release.name: Large probe release
big-probe-release.description: The carrier releases the large probe weeks before arrival.

small-probes-release.name: Small probes release
small-probes-release.description: The carrier releases the three small probes, aimed at widely spaced points.

big-probe-approach-and-entry.name: Large probe entry
big-probe-approach-and-entry.description: The large probe hits the top of the atmosphere behind its heat shield.

small-probes-approach-and-entry.name: Small probes entry
small-probes-approach-and-entry.description: The small probes hit the atmosphere at their separate points.

big-probe-descent-and-landing.name: Large probe descent
big-probe-descent-and-landing.description: Under a parachute and then free fall, the large probe measures all the way to the ground.

small-probes-landing.name: Small probes descent
small-probes-landing.description: The small probes fall through the clouds, reporting to the end.

interplanetary-bus-entry.name: Carrier entry
